articles.title: US midterm elections 2026: live results from Senate, House and governor races in all 50 states
articles.summary: With many seats still to come in, the Democrats have taken control of the Senate, House and several key governorships. Find live updating results in full here
articles.byline: Antonio Voce, Seán Clarke, Ed Gargan, Anna Leach and Ashley Kirk

blocks.text: Democrats*
*includes 2 independents
33/35 races called
Democrats
218 to win
First results expected after 18.00 EST (15.00 PST, 23.00 GMT, 10.00 AEST)

Most US election seats are reliably won by one party, so control of Congress comes down to a few competitive "battleground" seats. Experts track these to predict overall results; if a party wins seats they were expected to lose, it often signals a successful night. In the charts below, blue shapes on the right signal a good night for the Democrats, and red shapes on the left signal that the Republicans have done well.
Senate
See full results
Before the election, the Cook Report classified six Senate races as genuine "toss-ups". The Democrats need to win at least three of these, alongside the other races they are expected to win.
Likely DemocratLikely Dem.
Lean DemocratLean Dem.
Toss-upToss-up
Lean RepublicanLean Rep.
Likely RepublicanLikely Rep.
House

Democrats were favoured in enough House seats to take the chamber without winning any of the 18 seats the Cook Political Report classed as “toss-ups”. If they won every seat they were expected to win, they would comfortably win a majority. The balance of power rested on whether Democrats would hold the 18 seats rated “lean Democratic”. Republicans, favoured in 195 seats, would have needed to sweep all 18 toss-ups and flip five Democratic-leaning seats to win.

Thirty-three of the 100 members of the upper chamber were being elected regularly this year, along with two other special elections. Republicans had the Senate majority before the election. Senators serve six-year terms.
Election explained
Loading map...

Republicans were defending a majority in the 435-member House. Democrats held 212 House seats and needed 218 to win control. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms and face re-election every even year.

Gubernatorial elections were taking place in 36 states, as well as three territories. Republicans and Democrats held 18 of these state governorships each before the election. Three incumbent governors were retiring.
34/36 races called
How the elections work
The US legislature, Congress, has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate.
How is the House of Representatives elected and how do they work?
The lower chamber, the House of Representatives, has 435 voting seats, each representing a district of roughly similar size. There are elections for each of these seats every two years.

The speaker of the House is the chamber’s presiding officer, elected by the representatives. The House has several exclusive powers, such as the power to initiate revenue bills, impeach federal officials and elect the president in the case of an electoral college tie.
How is the Senate elected and how do they work?

The upper chamber, the Senate, has 100 members, who sit for six-year terms. One-third of the seats come up for election in each two-year cycle. Each state has two senators, regardless of its population; this means that Wyoming, with a population of less than 600,000, carries the same weight as California, with almost 40 million.

Most legislation needs to pass both chambers to become law, but the Senate has some important other functions, notably approving senior presidential appointments, for instance to the supreme court. The Senate also has the sole power to provide advice to the president, consent to ratify treaties and try impeachment cases for federal officials referred to it by the House.

In most states, the candidate with the most votes on election day wins the seat. However, Georgia and Louisiana require the winning candidate to garner 50% of votes cast; if no one does, they hold a runoff election between the top two candidates.

Maine and Alaska use ranked-choice voting as opposed to the first past the post voting system in congressional elections. Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the least-supported candidate is eliminated and their ballots are transferred to each voter’s next-ranked candidate. This continues until a candidate wins a majority.

In some states, an election can feature two candidates from the same party. Under top-two or “jungle” primary systems, candidates from all parties compete in the same primary and the two receiving the most votes advance, regardless of party. The congressional election candidates could both be Democrats or both be Republicans.

Florida and Ohio are having ‘special elections’ for the Senate because the previous holders of their seats – Marco Rubio and JD Vance – resigned to join the executive branch following the 2024 presidential election.
How are governors elected and how do they work?
Governors are elected by direct vote in their states. The candidate with the highest number of votes is declared the winner.
In every state, the executive branch is led by a governor. They serve for four years in office, with the exception of Vermont and New Hampshire where tenures are two years long.
Governors are responsible for implementing state laws, and have a range of powers available to them such as executive orders, executive budgets and legislative proposals and vetoes.
How are the results reported?

The election results on this page are reported by the Associated Press. AP will “call” the winner in a state when it determines that the trailing candidate has no path to victory. This can happen before 100% of votes in a state have been counted.
Estimates for the total vote in each state are also provided by AP. The numbers update throughout election night and in the following days, as more data on voter turnout becomes available.
Antonio Voce, Seán Clarke, Ed Gargan, Anna Leach and Ashley Kirk

blocks.text: The mother of a 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was fatally shot in the United States last week has left Ghana for America after being granted an emergency visa by President Donald Trump.

She said he had dreamt of becoming a medical doctor.
Her son, Javits Frimpong, was chased down and shot on Thursday morning on his way to school in the Bronx, New York.

Police have not made any arrests and an investigation is ongoing as authorities search for three teenage boys in connection with the shooting.
His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited the debate about gun violence in America.

articles.title: Endangered giant burrowing frog returns to wild after tadpoles rescued from ashes of black summer fires
articles.summary:
Tadpoles collected from puddles in East Gippsland were transported to Melbourne zoo, where they were raised to metamorphosis and successfully bred in captivity for the first time

After the…
articles.byline: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science

blocks.text: After the 2019-20 black summer bushfires, scientists in eastern Victoria stumbled across something they had been after for years: puddles of tadpoles from the southern giant burrowing frog, one of the state’s most cryptic amphibians.
The fires had torn through extensive areas in East Gippsland, sparking concerns for the survival of the frog, which is considered critically endangered in Victoria.
About 160 tadpoles were collected and transported to Melbourne zoo, where they were raised through to metamorphosis into frogs and successfully bred in captivity for the first time last year.

In a homecoming more than half a decade in the making, 53 of the original tadpoles – now male frogs about five years old – have been returned to their native habitat in a remote area of the state’s east.

The elusive frogs grow to roughly the size of a cricket ball in adulthood, and are believed to have long lifespans. Matt Clancy, a herpetologist at Snowline Ecology and an expert in the species, said that like other large frog species such as green tree frogs, giant burrowing frogs “could quite easily get over 20 years old”.
“Being such a large frog, you think they’d be easy to find, but they spend a lot of time buried underground in … sandy soils and forested environments.
“They will hunker down and not move at all until the next rains come and they emerge,” he said.

The frogs surface to breed in ephemeral creeks and ponds only when conditions are right. Tadpoles can take three months to two years to metamorphose, usually emerging as juvenile frogs in spring or summer, Clancy said.

blocks.caption: Southern giant burrowing frog returned to their native habitat

blocks.text: The 53 frogs were released immediately after big thunderstorms over the past several weeks at sites that had received 80 to 100mm of rain, he said.

Some of the released adults were not suitable for a captive breeding program run by Zoos Victoria. Ryan Moes, specialist amphibian keeper at Zoos Victoria, said the team conducted genetic testing on all the tadpoles originally collected.

“Within a breeding program, you don’t want to have all siblings breeding together,” he said. “The best thing to do was just to raise those frogs up and release them back out … into the wild once they were healthy frogs.”
Each frog was tagged before release, and song meters have been installed at release sites to detect the frogs’ calls.
Moes said the breeding program, which may involve future tadpole collections, ultimately aimed to ensure “those wild populations stay healthy and robust, and that the frog doesn’t go extinct”.
Giant burrowing frogs were split into two distinct subspecies – northern and southern – in 2021. Populations have been severely affected by habitat destruction and extreme climate events.
More frequent and severe bushfires and droughts due to climate change, as well as less rainfall, were ongoing existential threats, Moes said.
There are only five known breeding sites of southern giant burrowing frog in Victoria.

articles.title: Albanese government warned it’s ‘sleepwalking into another robodebt scenario’ over use of algorithms and AI
articles.summary:
Centre for Public Integrity report says mandatory audit and public register of all automated decision-making needed

  • Get our

blocks.text: The federal government is “sleepwalking its way into another robodebt” scandal amid a lack of transparency and legislation around use of algorithms and artificial intelligence in decisions, the chief executive of independent thinktank the Centre for Public Integrity said.
Dr Catherine Williams launched the centre’s “Computer Says No” report on Thursday, which examines the use of automated decision-making (ADM) tools by the government and calls for urgent reform.
The centre is concerned Australians may not know whether ADM has been used in decisions affecting them.

Among eight recommendations, the report calls for a mandatory audit and public register of all ADM use, and an independent oversight body with powers to monitor, audit and investigate the government over it.

Williams said the report was developed amid the centre’s increasing concern about the use of an algorithm as part of the government’s integrated assessment tool (IAT), which is used to assess the level of home support older Australians are entitled to.
The IAT has been found to be routinely under-assessing people’s needs and package entitlements, with aged care assessors banned by the government from overriding incorrect algorithmic decisions.

“We have been watching the evidence emerge in relation to the aged care algorithm tool, and becoming increasingly concerned about what is clearly the lack of an appropriate and robust framework to govern use of ADM by the government,” Williams said.

“It feels as though we are sleepwalking into another robodebt scenario, and that’s why we’ve decided to put this work forward now, in the hope also that it can help inform any framework that the government does propose in relation to ADM.”
The attorney general’s department has been developing an ADM framework, with public consultation ending in January 2025.

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, did not respond to questions about when a draft framework might be complete and made public but said the government “is committed to ensuring the safe and responsible use of ADM to deliver timely and efficient services for the Australian community”.
The framework will implement recommendations from the royal commission into robodebt, she said.

A report from the commonwealth ombudsman, published in October, found transparency recommendations from the robodebt royal commission had been ignored by the government in developing and rolling out the IAT.
after newsletter promotion

Rowland did not respond to questions about whether any ADM framework would be retrospective but said it “will be designed to improve accuracy and consistency of administrative decisions, embed robust safeguards, including transparency obligations, and ensure that ADM is used lawfully, responsibly, and with appropriate human oversight”.
The framework will also lift productivity and help deliver faster, more reliable services, she said.
In September, independent MP Kate Chaney introduced a private member’s bill to establish the first legislated, mandatory framework for ADM use by the government.
She said the attorney general department’s consultation process for an ADM framework “finished almost two years ago”.
“I have met with the attorney general about it and they say ‘We’re working on it’. I think it’s really important that we keep the pressure up so that it doesn’t get dropped because it’s too hard.”
Chaney said government departments are making decisions about ADM use with little consistency or transparency.
“The government wants to find cost savings in the public service and automating decision-making can be a way of achieving those savings,” she said.

“But I think trust in the government is low. There does need to be transparency about when decisions are automated, and when it’s not appropriate for those to be automated, for people to be able to get a clear understanding of why the decision was made and to be really clear about what the pathways are to review that decision.
“This is what people expect of government.”

articles.title: Australia has an especially bad inflation problem. So why are we only middle-of-the pack on the misery index?
articles.summary:
Comparing Australia to other countries may not be much comfort but does offer some perspective on the economy

  • Get our

blocks.text: Is Australia’s inflation problem worse than the rest of the world’s?
A day after the Reserve Bank delivered its fifth interest rate hike for the year, increasingly stressed mortgage holders would be justified asking.
For Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, the answer is easy.
“Our inflation problem is worse than in other countries, that is very clear,” Kearns says.
The stats tell the story.
Consumer prices on average climbed by 4.3% in the year to September, and are anticipated to climb even faster by year’s end.
A quick survey of other advanced countries, and the eurozone, shows none with inflation near our level.
So far, so bad.
But before we break out the pitchforks, there is an important nuance that’s worth appreciating.
While our cost of living here is rising faster than in comparable countries, our labour market is stronger.
“Our performance in unemployment has been much better than in New Zealand, Canada and in Europe, and that is a positive thing for Australia,” Kearns says.
So should we be upset about having higher inflation than other countries, or relatively satisfied that our labour market has remained strong?
In other words: is the economic pain experienced greater here than in, say, New Zealand or Canada?
after newsletter promotion
A very crude way of answering what is a complex question is the so-called “misery index”.
The concept was thought up by an American economist, Arthur Okun, in the 1970s – when it became popular enough to be weaponised during the 1976 presidential campaign.
The idea is simple: add the rates of unemployment and inflation together to create a very high level view of what households are experiencing.
By this measure, Australia goes from worst of the lot for inflation, to middle-of-the pack in overall misery.
That may not be much comfort, but it does provide some perspective to this challenging economic time we are living through.

articles.title: ‘Discontent and distrust’: annual social cohesion checkup shows exactly what’s making Australia angry
articles.summary:
Cost of living and AI outrank climate change and war as top concerns for future, but support for multiculturalism remains strong

  • Get our

blocks.text: The vast majority of Australians support immigration and multiculturalism despite more feeling poorer – and increasingly pessimistic and distrustful of government, the annual Scanlon report on social cohesion has revealed.
People are more worried about artificial intelligence than climate change or going to war, but a global economic downturn and cost-of-living pressures are Australians’ key concerns.

Economic pain is also changing the way people vote, with people suffering hardship jumping ship to One Nation, according to the report, which is one of the country’s most extensive social research projects.

But, despite rising concern about antisemitism and Islamophobia, social cohesion in Australia has actually remained steady. The lead author of the report concedes many findings are cause for concern, but notes support for multiculturalism and diversity remains high, as does the sense of connection Australians feel to their communities.

“People are clearly under pressure with economic pressures, there’s discontent and distrust, people are blaming immigration … but we don’t necessarily see a permanence to that,” said Dr James O’Donnell from the Australian National University.
“It’s not just that people are getting angry generally. They’re really under pressure and that plays out in different ways.”
More than 10,000 Australians were asked 100 questions by the Scanlon Foundation on topics ranging from life satisfaction and financial circumstances to voting intent.
The report found happiness had declined most for millennials and generation Xers.
The headline figure, the Scanlon index of social cohesion, remained at 78 out of 100 – a consistent figure since 2023.
The philanthropy organisation calculates this number through data about Australians’ sense of belonging, worth, social inclusion and justice, participation in society, and attitudes about acceptance.

“The really important stuff for social cohesion – the sense of belonging and acceptance – a lot of that is built into our daily life. There’s a resilience to that; we’re still volunteering, there’s a high level of trust in the people around us and local communities,” O’Donnell said.
But Scanlon concedes this headline number can “disguise” important shifts in individual numbers, including “increasing strain on Australia’s social cohesion”.
Despite the index remaining static, 62% of adults believe social cohesion has declined in recent years.
Australians pessimistic about their lives
Nearly one-third of respondents expect their lives to get worse over the next four years. That’s up from 29% last year.

While 79% of people said they had been happy in the past year – a number which has remained stable since 2021 – 48% said they were pessimistic about Australia’s future. That figure is up from 43% in 2025.
The Scanlon report said happiness had declined the most for millennials (born between 1981 and 1996) and gen X (born 1965-1980).

“Since 2014, the proportion of Millennials who are happy or very happy declined from 84% to 75%, while the proportion who are unhappy or very unhappy increased from 16% to 25%. Among Gen X, the proportion who are unhappy or very unhappy increased from 19% to 23%,” the report said.
“Across all generations, people are increasingly pessimistic about their future.”

Cost of living was by far the most-cited issue facing Australia, with 36% of people rating it as their top issue. Housing affordability and shortages was second on 11%, other economic issues on 10% and immigration on 9%.
On a different measure, about “major issues” facing the nation, 77% of Australians were concerned about a severe global economic downturn.
Scanlon warned many Australians were facing financial stress in ways which were “likely harmful to social cohesion”.

Some 20% of adults were unhappy with their financial situation. While 10% described themselves as “poor”, 13% said they had gone without food at least sometimes, and struggled to pay their rent or mortgage on time.
after newsletter promotion

About one in five reported they sometimes had to go without medicine or healthcare, could not afford to heat or cool their homes, or had to ask friends or family to borrow money. Another 16% said they’d had to sell possessions because they needed cash.
Immigration and multiculturalism
While the social cohesion index remained steady, several key measures of cultural diversity have eroded.
Negative attitudes toward Indian immigrants rose to 33% in 2026, up from 25% in 2024.
In new questions asked in 2026, 36% of people said they had a negative attitude toward immigrants from Israel, 39% toward immigrants from Palestine and 41% toward those from Iran.
Some 18% reported a negative attitude toward Jewish people, up from 13% in 2024, while 43% said the same of Muslim people, up from 33% in 2024.
Negative attitudes to Hindus (17%, up from 13%) and Sikhs (20%, up from 14%) also rose since 2024, while negativity toward Christians dropped from 19% to 13%.

But public support for multiculturalism, despite a toxic political debate, remains very high. Some 87% of Australians believe immigrants are just as likely to be “good citizens” as Australian-born people, 76% agreed multiculturalism has been good for the nation and 73% agreed immigrants were good for the economy.
What is keeping Australians up at night?

After cost of living (36%), Australians’ top issues fell away quickly, to housing (11%), economic issues and immigration. The environment and climate change was the top issue for just 4% of people, with national security and terrorism at 1%, alongside health and education, social media, misinformation and artificial intelligence.

When asked about “major issues” facing Australia, 77% were concerned or very concerned about a global economic downturn. Despite only 1% rating it among their top issues, another 69% said they were worried about artificial intelligence – that ranked above climate change (55%) and a military conflict involving Australia (51%).
What does it mean for politics?

The report cross-references various figures with voting intention. It finds financial hardship may be contributing to support eroding for the Labor and Coalition parties, suggesting people feeling economic pain were more likely to vote One Nation or Greens.

This year, 42% of current Greens voters and 35% of those backing One Nation had gone without meals or healthcare, missed repayments, or couldn’t heat or cool their homes. That compared to only 24% of Labor voters and 23% of Coalition voters.
The Scanlon report found this is changing votes.

“Among people who voted for Labor or the Coalition at the 2025 federal election, we estimate that 47% who are experiencing financial hardship now prefer some other party or candidate compared with 36% of people who reported no hardship,” it said, with most of that vote shifting to One Nation.
In related findings, the report found that across all voting groups, “people experiencing financial stress are predicted to have substantially weaker trust in institutions”.

Political polarisation is also a feature of the report, with markedly different perceptions of society depending on voting intent. Only 9% of One Nation voters trust the federal government to do the right thing, and just one-third believe elections are fair and that courts make fair decisions.

That compares with 54% of Labor, 35% of Coalition and 25% of Greens voters trusting the government to do the right thing; 81% of Labor and 63% each of Greens and Coalition voters believing elections are fair; and 68% of Labor, 57% of Coalition and 54% of Greens voters believing courts make fair decisions.
Only 16% of Labor voters believe government leaders abuse their powers, compared to 64% of One Nation voters.

articles.title: Muslim Votes Matter softens anti-Labor stance ahead of Victorian election in bid to defeat One Nation in at-risk seats
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Advocacy group will put volunteers on the ground in Labor-held outer suburban seats that could swing towards Pauline Hanson’s party

  • Get our

blocks.text: Muslim Votes Matter will relax its anti-Labor position at this month’s Victorian election, putting volunteers on the ground in key outer suburban seats the incumbent government risks losing to One Nation.

The grassroots advocacy group will direct its supporters to vote for Labor ahead of Pauline Hanson’s party in all lower house Victorian electorates and will aim to have volunteers on the ground in the seats of Greenvale, in Melbourne’s north, and Narre Warren South, in the city’s south-east, which the party fears could be seized by One Nation.

This is a departure from its position at last year’s federal election, where the pro-Palestine group focused on endorsing Greens and independent candidates to punish Labor, prompted by anger over the federal government’s handling of Israel’s war in Gaza.
Ghaith Krayem, the national spokesperson for MVM, said “circumstances have changed” ahead of the state election on 28 November.
But Krayem said the group would still not put Labor in the top spot in any seat on its how-to-vote cards, instead favouring independents and minor parties as it did at the 2025 federal election.
“As a community, we certainly don’t want to increase One Nation’s influence,” he said.
“There is a risk that if we went hard anti-Labor, like we did in the federal election, that would in fact benefit One Nation, and that’s not an outcome we want.”

Krayem said Muslim communities feared that if the Coalition was unable to form majority government, it could be forced to negotiate with One Nation and agree to some of its policy demands. He pointed to Hanson calling for a burqa ban in Australia as rhetoric that affected Muslim people.
“It becomes more normal for people to question the rights of how Muslims dress, to question the rights of whether the Muslim community is Australian enough,” he said.
“That is not a good place for the country or for the state.”

Krayem said MVM would preference Labor over the Liberal party in seats where preferences from the latter could flow to One Nation. The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, has been tight lipped when asked about preferences or potential deals with One Nation, saying the Coalition is running for majority government.
Greenvale, a seat created before the 2022 election and held by Labor on a 7.1% margin on a two-party preferred basis, has a significant Middle Eastern population.

“Given that it has a significant Muslim population, we think if we’re on the ground in Greenvale, we can shore up a bit of that support and minimise the risk of Greenvale becoming a One Nation seat,” Krayem said.
after newsletter promotion
Labor holds Narre Warren South on a 8.3% two-party preferred margin and data from the 2021 census shows 13.1% of the constituency are Muslim compared to 4.2% state-wide.
MVM will also have volunteers on the ground in Tarneit, where 14.6% of residents in the electorate are Muslim. Labor holds the seat on a 12.3% margin.
Krayem said the outer western electorate was selected as a target seat following conversations with Muslim communities who said they were frustrated with Labor.
“Labor’s views with respect to Palestine, freedom of speech, protesting, all of those things, is still very much an issue across the community,” he said.
“Palestine and Gaza is still the number-one issue that our community is unhappy about at all levels of government.”

MVM will create how-to-vote cards for every lower and upper house seat based on how candidates align with its policy priorities, and volunteers will hand out the cards at polling booths in Greenvale, Narre Warren South and Tarneit. MVM’s Victorian policy priorities include tackling Islamophobia, cost of living and housing security, and respecting the rights of residents to advocate for Palestine.

articles.title: ICC may still hold confirmation of charges vs. Bato despite absence --counsel
articles.summary: The ICC could still hold its confirmation of charges against Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa despite his still being on the run, a lawyer for Duterte-era drug war victims said.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 9:56pm

The International Criminal Court (ICC) could still hold its confirmation of charges against Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa despite his still being on the run, a lawyer for Duterte-era drug war victims said.

In a 24 Oras report from Mariz Umali on Wednesday, ICC Assistant to Counsel Kristina Conti said that the tribunal could still hold a confirmation of charges hearing against Dela Rosa as an indirect co-perpetrator in former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war.

“Pwedeng magkaroon kasi ng confirmation of charges hearing in the absence of the suspect. Nangyari yun last September lang, sa kaso ni Joseph Kony na hindi nila matukoy-tukoy kung nasaan, pero ang tagal na nakabinbin yung kaso. So, sa confirmation of charges hearing, posibleng absent yung akusado,” Conti said.

(There could be a confirmation of charges hearing in the absence of the suspect. That happened just in September, in the case of Joseph Kony, who cannot be found, but the case has been lodged for so long. So, in the confirmation of charges hearing, the accused could be absent.)
According to the Rome Statute, the confirmation of charges could be done against the accused if they could not be found or if they are trying to escape.
However, the accused must have a lawyer present to represent them, with the Pretrial Chamber Judges needing to approve of the matter as well.

This is what happened in September 2025 when the confirmation of charges were held against Kony, a Ugandan warlord. He faces 39 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity. The ICC had issued an arrest warrant against him in 2005 but he could not be found.

“Ang sabihin ng court, masyadong matagal na tayong naghihintay para sa paghuli nitong ganitong suspect. Kaya may hihiling dyan na pwede bang mag-proceed kami without the presence of the suspect,” Conti said.
(The court will say that we have been waiting too long for this suspect. So there is a plea to proceed without the presence of the suspect.)
Conti said that in the view of victims, these movements are still important and that it at least showed the case moving.

Dela Rosa has been on the run even before the ICC put out the arrest warrant for him in May. The senator was Duterte’s former police chief during the drug war, which saw the deaths of at least 6,000 people. — Jean Mangaluz/BM, GMA News

articles.title: Over 100 more dead pets found dumped in San Jose Del Monte, Bulacan
articles.summary: More than 100 additional dead pets have been found dumped at various locations across San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 9:56pm
More than 100 additional dead pets have been found dumped at various locations across San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.
In a "24 Oras" report from Bea Pinlac on Wednesday, pets were found in varying states of decay across the city. Some of the bodies were already riddled with worms.
“Most are too degraded and unidentifiable… we’re looking at probably around 120 bags or more,” said Chris Taylor, the founder of Luna and Furry Siblings Animal Welfare Rescue.
“One of the places that we suspect — they take from other vet clinics, other places, crematories that do not do their actual cremations. They contract out. So again, we’re not really sure,” he added.
The animal foundation is already working with the National Bureau of Investigation to retrieve the remains of the pets.

“This is on too large a scale. We're going to need the city, CENRO (City Environment and Natural Resources Office) and public health out here, because it’s just too massive and we’re going to need too many people to search the whole area, so really, it’s just going to be a manpower issue,” Taylor said.
This new dumping site was preceded by the initial site found in San Jose del Monte. The first dumping site was tied to a pet crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite.

“Titingnan yung composition; is it really yung ash coming from pets, animals or baka hindi… It will be up to the owners if they want to air their side… Kung wala naman po talaga siyang maling ginawa, face the music, give your side sa ating mga investigators… As of now, what we can see is possibly estafa plus civil damages,” Philippine National Police (PNP) spokesperson Col. Allen Rae Co said.

(We will see the composition; is it really ash coming from pets, animals, or maybe not… It will be up to the owners if they want to air their side… If they really did nothing wrong, face the music, give your side to our investigators… As of now, what we can see is possibly estafa plus civil damages.) —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Fleabag creator donates flat to help early-career writers live in London
articles.summary:
Phoebe Waller-Bridge joins stars signing up to scheme tackling class barriers in theatre

Phoebe Waller-Bridge has donated a London flat so that early-career writers can afford to live in the…
articles.byline: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent

blocks.text: Phoebe Waller-Bridge has donated a London flat so that early-career writers can afford to live in the capital.

The creator of the hit show Fleabag bought the property specifically for Writers’ Block, a new scheme which tackles class barriers in theatre. The flat will be offered to writers from disadvantaged backgrounds, who will pay only the bills. Waller-Bridge has also made what the initiative described as a “generous financial contribution”.
The screenwriter Jack Thorne, who co-created Adolescence and wrote Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, is also backing the scheme financially.
“I was lucky when I started out, my brother lived in Croydon and was able to put me up,” he said. “He did so, rather selflessly, for five years, before I moved to Luton and he got his peace.

“For many writers, the need for a roof makes writing impossible, which is why this pilot is so important. If we want stories told about our complicated world, we need writers of every background writing them.
“If you’re from privilege, your biggest problem is what to fill a page with. If you’re not, so much of your struggle is about the need to survive.”

blocks.caption: Mark Stanley, Owen Cooper and Stephen Graham in Adolescence. The Netflix show’s writer, Jack Thorne, says he was lucky to have accommodation in London when starting his career. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Other backers include: the playwright and screenwriter James Graham, who wrote stage shows including Ink, Quiz and Dear England; Happy Valley creator Sally Wainwright; The Crown’s Peter Morgan; and Waller-Bridge’s partner Martin McDonagh, who wrote and directed films including The Banshees of Inisherin and Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri.

Research by the Sutton Trust and the Creative Industries Policy and Evidence Centre found that just 16% of people working in the creative industries came from working-class backgrounds. It also found that class imbalances were more pronounced in the sector than in any other.

Graham said the industry’s efforts to improve representation continued to overlook class. “The industry’s urgent pursuit of representation is still letting down the biggest area of under-representation of all, which is class,” he said.

“When I first made it to London, I slept on friends’ floors and worked in call centres and bars while I wrote. Every spare room a scheme like this can give to writers starting out in London, not only helps them write but saves them from giving up completely.”
after newsletter promotion

Writers’ Block grew out of the Adopt a Playwright Award, founded in 2008 by Sofie Mason and Diana Jervis-Read to provide affordable accommodation for writers who need to be in London for meetings, rehearsals, performances and career opportunities.

The scheme invites Londoners to offer spare rooms at reduced rates, capped at £30 a night or £500 a month. It has signed up 15 homes and helped 12 writers find accommodation, from overnight stays to longer-term placements.
The organisers say the scheme could appeal to older people living alone who would welcome companionship and extra income but feel uncomfortable advertising a room to strangers.

articles.title: UNHCR criticises UK’s 30-year ‘earned settlement’ plans for refugees
articles.summary: Home secretary Shabana Mahmood maintains rigorous rules for those who arrive on small boats

blocks.text: The United Nations refugee agency has said a government plan to make refugees wait up to 30 years before they get permission to settle in the UK “raises significant concerns”.

The strategy was unveiled earlier this week by Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, as she announced a softening of aspects of her immigration plans, but kept some of the rigorous rules drawn up by her office last year.

Mahmood introduced a carve-out for care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years, but maintained rules to make those who arrived by irregular means such as small boats having to wait up to 30 years.

UNHCR, which has international responsibility for refugees, told the Guardian that the plan to increase the time people who arrived by irregular means have to wait before being able to apply for settlement was “likely to be detrimental”.

Some refugees can reduce the upper limit of 30 years if they enter work or study but there is a 10-year penalty for those who arrive on small boats or concealed in lorries rather than arriving via safe and legal routes. The government has significantly reduced the latter and although they have announced some legal routes they will only be able to be accessed by a small minority of people seeking sanctuary here.

The UNHCR welcomed the legal routes but said: “An extended qualifying period for settlement for refugees raises significant concerns particularly when considered alongside the introduction of short term stay arrangements and changes made last year that would preclude many from ever accessing citizenship. Taken together, these measures are likely to be detrimental to refugees’ sense of security, belonging and stability, and to impact their ability to contribute and become part of their new communities.

“Refugees are not migrants: they have fled their countries because they cannot rely on their protection nor safely return home. For refugees, safety means more than a grant of asylum and settlement has an important role to play.”

Kamena Dorling, director of policy at Helen Bamber Foundation, also raised concerns about the 30-year rule. She said: “We are deeply alarmed and disappointed by the government’s announcement on ‘earned settlement’. It will cause profound and lasting harm to refugees, including survivors of torture, trafficking and other forms of extreme cruelty.

“The government had an opportunity to change its approach after receiving extensive evidence about the devastating consequences of this policy but instead has doubled down on its approach that will damage the lives and futures of thousands of men, women, families and children, as well as harm wider integration and social cohesion.
She said that extending the qualifying period for settlement “is simply inhumane”.

She added: “This will not deter people fleeing war, persecution, torture and violence, who are fighting for their lives and seeking safety in the UK. When legal routes are so severely limited, people will continue to take desperate measures to reach safety. It will punish people who have already endured unimaginable harm, leaving those recognised as refugees facing decades of uncertainty, insecurity and fear.”

articles.title: Joy in Iran over ‘Trump’s defeat’ in US midterm elections – but war is not over
articles.summary: Iran celebrates its claimed role in ‘regime change’ amid pressure on US president to ‘finish the job’ with attack

blocks.text: Iran this week unveiled a massive new billboard and banners over Enqelab Square in central Tehran. The billboard pledged in English: “We will kill Trump” – elevating the degree of personal animus with which Donald Trump is viewed in official Iranian circles.

The poster depicts the US president behind bars with his head bowed. And in a sense, given the US midterm election results on Tuesday, Iran has indeed killed Trump, or at least the second term of his presidency. Trump’s reverse is all the more piquant because it comes on the day Iran’s leadership celebrates the anniversary of the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran in 1979, an event that ensnared Jimmy Carter, and a reminder of how Iran has ruined the prospects of more than one US president.
Not surprisingly, the keenly followed election results have led to a good degree of triumphalism inside Iran.

Ehsan Movaheidian, an international relations scholar, claimed: “The Islamic Republic of Iran has succeeded in regime change in America. The same will soon happen in Europe as well. Bow down before the power of Iran.”

Meisam Zohurian, a conservative member of parliament, said: “The joy over the outcome of the US elections has nothing to do with the arrival of this party or the departure of that party. The issue is the aggressor was smeared in the dirt and Iran had an impact on the result.”
Ali Nikzad, the first deputy speaker of the parliament, said: “These electoral defeats are the aftershocks of Trump’s defeat by the Iranian people.”

blocks.caption: A student walks over Israeli and US flags during a rally on Wednesday marking the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the US embassy, outside the former embassy in Tehran. Photograph: Sobhan Farajvan/Pacific Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Iran’s supreme leader said anyone expecting a shift in US policy was “seriously mistaken”, however. “Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Mojtaba Khamenei wrote.
Others predicted further electoral defeats for what they considered to be the warmongers in Europe, and the expulsion of US bases from the entire Middle East.

The resistance – or bloody-mindedness – shown by Iran for the past eight gruelling months did allow the strait of Hormuz to become an Iranian-controlled channel through which inflation and high diesel prices were transmitted to the American system. Even Trump himself on Wednesday accepted, and lamented, that the American people had decided the “short-term” pain of inflation was not a price worth paying to prevent Iran becoming a nuclear power.

But the big question now is whether either side will regard these seismic results as a moment to review their diplomatic strategy. Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, was quick to call on Trump to accept the wisdom of the American people. On social media he urged Trump to bow to the verdict of America: “Whether driven by conscience or the cost of living, America said no to war and we endorse this message.”
Ghalibaf added: “If the US government betrays the public will in order to serve international paymasters and blackmailers it will learn our ‘no’ comes with a nightmare.”

Yet Iran will also be asked to reflect on the wisdom of war by the Gulf monarchies, and possibly by Russia and China – the latter a country that seems finally to be stirring itself to find a solution to the blockade in the strait of Hormuz that is preventing badly-needed Middle East oil exports from reaching its industries.

China tends to knock only on doors that it knows are going to open, so it is probably testing the feasibility of a deal in which Iran “downblends” – or dilutes – its stockpile of highly enriched uranium inside Iran under international supervision. A Chinese special envoy is travelling to Oman, Iran and Saudi Arabia almost immediately.

These countries, some sympathetic to Iran’s predicament, can point out that if Tehran ever thought in the run-up to the elections Trump would capitulate and turn his carrier fleet around, it was mistaken. Some Iranian diplomats had indeed hoped that the prospect of defeat in the midterms, and pressure from within the Republican party, would have led Trump to make concessions to Tehran.
after newsletter promotion

In fact, both sides and the chief mediator, Qatar, clearly did try to use polling day as a lever, but in the end neither side retreated. Trump, for once, was true to his word and refused to allow the darkening opinion polls to reduce his determination to keep Iran in his vice. Confined to a holding bay of “neither war nor peace”, Trump’s priority was to keep the oil price as low as possible by repeatedly suggesting a settlement might be imminent.

For the next two months before the new Congress convenes in January – so reducing his budgetary options – Trump has greater latitude, and little accountability. The damage to the Republican party has been done and cannot be undone.

Unsurprisingly the Trump influencers who advocated for the war in the first place are piling on pressure to strike again quickly. Laura Loomer wrote on X: “Time for President Trump to deal with Iran once and for all. Just do it, Nothing to lose now. Finish the job.”

But the credibility of Loomer and her like has been severely damaged: in February, she had advised Trump that regime change in Iran – “a little excursion” – could be as easy as knocking over the Maduro regime in Venezuela. Similarly, Benjamin Netanyahu is now touting intelligence showing that Iran is preparing to use chemical weapons. The ease with which the Israeli prime minister conjures up intelligence to justify another assault on Iran may by now have struck the White House.

Hillary Clinton, Trump’s old sparring partner, is one who thinks Trump will probably launch the long-delayed attack. She said: “I think he will feel trapped. He will feel angry and resentful and he will react aggressively.”

Having come so far, and paid so high a political price, Trump may in the next two months try to secure a legacy by finishing the job – however he defines that. He is convinced, as he told Fox News this week, that “Iran has very few missiles and drones left, and even less capacity to build any more”. He crowed: “We are dealing with total strength. We can end it any time.”
Unfortunately, such blithe optimism has been heard before.

articles.title: Investigators say they found tail pieces of Learjet that crashed in Florida, killing nine
articles.summary:
National Transportation Safety Board says discovery of parts confirms plane was breaking apart before it crashed

A piece of the private Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida, killing all nine…

blocks.text: A piece of the private Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida, killing all nine people onboard, was found 4 miles (6km) away from the crash site, according to investigators on Tuesday, providing confirmation the plane was breaking apart prior to impact.

The majority of the left elevator, part of the tail that controls the pitch of the aircraft, was found in three separate pieces between 1.3 miles and 3.8 miles from the crash site at Greenacres, near West Palm Beach, according to National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman.

“What that means exactly, in terms of what caused the aircraft to lose control, or whether the loss of this piece was a result of the forces on the aircraft, we don’t know yet,” Chapman said at a news conference.
Chapman said without the elevator intact, the pilot would not have been able to pull the aircraft out of its nosedive.

“At those speeds I don’t know that it would’ve been effective even if it had still been attached to the aircraft, but knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us toward other things to investigate,” Chapman added.

The jet was flying from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas on Sunday when it appears to have flown into a thunderstorm at 35,000ft, causing – according to radio transmissions from co-pilot Nathalia Filgueiras – icing on the jet and turbulence, causing it to climb and fall by more than 700ft before it began to dive.
Filgueiras reportedly texted her boyfriend before the situation turned critical: “I’ve got turbulence, I’ve got ice.”

She also told air traffic controllers that the plane was descending at 8,000ft per minute, then 10,000ft per minute. During one of her final transmissions she said: “Declare an emergency 722 Bravo Delta, we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute.”
Seconds later, it crashed in to the ground near a trailer park and exploded into a fireball at the intersection of Military Trail and Cresthaven Boulevard in Palm Beach.
Chapman said weather would be a key initial focus of the investigation into the crash.

The victims of the crash have been identified by relatives as technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; and their two young children. Family friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr also died in the crash, as did the family’s nanny, Anita Maria Cetina.

The pilot of the plane has been identified as 55-year-old Jeff Gregory by his employer, East Coast Jets, a charter aviation company based in Allentown, Pennsylvania. “Our prayers go out to Jeff’s family, his fellow crew member, the passengers and everyone affected by this heart breaking tragedy,” the company said in a statement.
In the NTSB briefing on Tuesday, Chapman encouraged anyone living in the area to leave any pieces that may look as if they belong to the aircraft alone and to contact the NTSB or local authorities.
He said the NTSB would work to lay out the recovered pieces of the plane in a way that “remakes” the aircraft in order to determine what may have occurred.

Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti told the Associated Press that the pieces that broke off the aircraft were probably a result of the nosedive, not the cause, claiming the pieces found close to the crash site indicate they likely fell off closer to the ground.
“If those parts would have broken off at altitude, those pieces would be a lot farther away,” Guzzetti said.
Freeze frames from videos appear to show the entire horizontal stabilizer missing from the Learjet’s tail prior to impact.

Former NTSB member John Goglia said flight tracking data appears to show the aircraft leveling off for about eight seconds at about 8,000ft (2,438 meters) prior to its nosedive to the ground. He said he believes the key tail pieces likely came off when the captain of the plane attempted to pull up sharply.
“He apparently leveled off for brief moments at 8,000ft and to accomplish that he likely overstressed the tail and the horizontal stabilizer separated from the airplane,” Goglia said.
A preliminary report describing what happened will be released in about a month, but it will likely take more than a year to determine the exact cause of the crash.

articles.title: 'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
articles.summary: Some Republicans tell the BBC the president's focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost them.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The result amounted to a rejection of Trump, one top Republican lobbyist said
ByDaniel Bush
Washington correspondent
Inside the Republican Party, initial shock at the stunning election results on Tuesday night quickly gave way to anger with US President Donald Trump.

After Democrats won upset after upset in deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, some Republicans focused their ire on Trump, arguing that his focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost the party control of Congress.

"It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told the BBC. "This is a disaster of the first magnitude. Nobody saw it coming like this."
Most Republicans expected to lose control of the House and were clear-eyed about the challenge of holding onto the Senate in a tough election cycle that favoured the party out of power.
But some said in interviews that Trump dragged them down with unpopular policies, a low job approval rating and obsession over construction projects in Washington.
"It was just one mistake after another," said Gregg Peppin, a Republican strategist in Minnesota. "Clearly, in state after state, people did not like the president's policies."
A White House ally said public disapproval with Trump over the Iran war, tariffs and the administration's immigration crackdown created a "perfect storm" in November.
"There's palpable frustration [within] the party about how this has all played out," the person said, and much of it is directed at Trump. Anger with Trump "is extremely high".

items: FOLLOW LIVE: Election results and analysis of the US midterms
Anthony Zurcher: Democrats push deep into Trump heartland
Key moments from a night of midterm election firsts
Five reasons why Trump did so badly

blocks.text: The BBC spoke to a dozen party operatives, campaign officials, White House allies and others, many of whom spoke on background to offer a candid assessment of Trump's approach to the midterms.

Trump and Republicans had a lot riding on the outcome on Tuesday night. A stronger showing by the president's party - as happened in 2022, when Democrats under then-President Joe Biden lost just nine seats in the House, and gained one in the Senate - would have given Republicans some momentum heading into 2028.
But Trump will instead face a motivated Democratic majority in Congress that is eager to investigate the administration, block his judicial nominees and stymie the rest of his agenda.
The midterms have ushered in an uncertain new phase in Trump's second term and may force Republicans to start grappling with their post-Trump future.
Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results

"I don't think his influence is slipping," said Steve Scheffler, the Republican National Committeeman in Iowa, speaking on the eve of the election. Still, he said, when it came to the midterms, "there were things you wish he said differently".
Trump was silent for much of the night before posting a message on Truth Social after the House and Senate were called for Democrats.
"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote.

He said in later interviews with the New York Times and Fox News that he would accept the election results. Trump told Fox he was a "little bit surprised" by the election results, but noted that the president's party typically fared poorly in midterm elections.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Republican Senator Jon Husted at an election event in Ohio, where the Senate seat flipped in favour of Democrat Sherrod Brown

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Republican Senator Jon Husted at an election event in Ohio, where the Senate seat flipped in favour of Democrat Sherrod Brown

Since 1934, the party in the White House has only gained seats in three midterm elections. While the Democratic gains in 2026 did not set a record, the party did win dozens of House races, state governor contests and Senate seats, including in states where the party had not been competitive for decades.

Before Tuesday, Democrats had not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, and had not won a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. The party also notched surprise upsets in other reliably red states like South Carolina that were thought to be safe seats for Republicans just weeks before Election Day.

Trump and Vice-President JD Vance held dozens of campaign rallies in the run-up to the midterms. The principal Trump-aligned Super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent hundreds of millions backing Republican candidates.

Trump allies said it was unfair to hold him responsible for the party's election losses. They pointed to the history of midterm elections, and said the party was saddled with weak Republican candidates in battleground states like Georgia, Michigan and Texas.

Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, ran "the worst Senate campaign in the country from either side of the aisle," said another Texas Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. "If Ken's campaign knocked on 100,000 doors I'd be shocked," the source said. The person added that Paxton's victorious Democratic opponent, James Talarico, ran "a really good and smart campaign."
Others defended Trump's autumn campaign schedule, noting that he had to balance his day job of running the country with midterm travel.

"He's the president. He's not going to spend his time campaigning 24/7," said Krish Mathrani, the Michigan Republican Party's youth chair. Mathrani said Trump's campaign rallies helped drive up enthusiasm among Republican voters. "President Trump is a turnout machine," he said.
That's true in presidential elections. But Trump's vaunted turnout operation has failed to deliver in elections when he's not on the ballot, and 2026 proved no different.

Voters rejected Trump's argument that the economy was better on his watch and that he was achieving his aims in the war with Iran. The effort by Trump to portray Democrats as extreme socialists also fell flat, as voters handed victories to moderates like Roy Cooper in North Carolina.
"That just didn't work with Cooper," said a Cooper campaign official. "Trying to tag him as some socialist liberal, that wasn't going to fly."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Republican supporters at a watch party in Iowa, where Democrat candidate Josh Turek won a Senate seat

blocks.text: Republican supporters at a watch party in Iowa, where Democrat candidate Josh Turek won a Senate seat
Trump often seemed disinterested in the midterms over the summer, the period of time when Republicans in Congress shifted their focus to the election.

Trump was consumed by the war with Iran abroad and his construction overhaul of Washington at home. The projects included the under-construction ballroom and a helipad on the South Lawn of the White House, renovations to a local golf course, a proposed memorial arch near Arlington Cemetery and renovations to the Kennedy Center.

Events like a UFC match at the White House on Trump's 80th birthday in June created the impression that the president was more interested in feting himself than winning the midterms, several sources said. Trump also repeatedly downplayed the rising costs of gas and often cast the affordability issue as a Democratic hoax.

Trump turned his full attention to the election in September at the Republican Party's midterm convention. The event was a gamble: Republicans hadn't held a midterm convention in decades, and it was an open question whether voters would tune in.
Trump dominated the convention in Dallas, frustrating Republicans who told the BBC they wanted to highlight the party's midterm candidates.

In his rambling keynote speech, Trump pledged to give $5,000 (£3,700) to anyone who voted for Republicans and raised eyebrows with an endorsement of Paxton which included a lengthy criticism of the candidate's lack of charisma and physical appearance.

"Obviously, that's never helpful," Robin Armstrong, Texas' Republican National Committeeman, said of Trump's critique of Paxton. "You're not going to stop what President Trump says. We just have to kind of live with that."

The convention failed to attract a large television audience, and Democrats were quick to call it a failure. "It backfired for Republicans because nobody paid any attention to it," said Terri Burke, the Texas Democratic Party's executive director.

Trump's penchant for straying off-message continued when he hit the campaign trail in the final weeks before Election Day. He made headlines for praising Ohio Republican Senator John Husted's physique, and drew criticism for calling El-Sayed a "jihadist" in the Michigan Senate race.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mike Rogers in Michigan was among the other losing candidates - having been beaten to a Senate seat by Democrat Abdul El-Sayed

blocks.text: Mike Rogers in Michigan was among the other losing candidates - having been beaten to a Senate seat by Democrat Abdul El-Sayed

As Trump criss-crossed the country stumping for Republican candidates, the White House contended with controversies in Washington. Katie Zacharia was ousted after just five days as White House press secretary, and Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as the US ambassador to Greece after reports surfaced that she asked a donor to pay her credit card debt.

Trump also faced a backlash in October for striking a deal to buy Russian diesel. The agreement, which blindsided members of Congress and drew condemnation from some Republicans, came just weeks after Trump signed a sanctions bill aimed at cutting off Russian oil and gas revenue.

Democrats used the deal and other scandals swirling around the White House to make the case for retaking control of Congress. The messaging resonated in the end, as Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress in convincing fashion.
A second White House ally said that the president's political aides projected optimism until the final days of the election, even as it became clear the party was headed to defeat.
Now, as Republicans take stock of the loss, several said they were ready to look ahead to the 2028 election.
"Whether that's JD Vance, or Macro Rubio, or Ted Cruz, we've got a pretty big bench," said Scheffler, the state's RNC member. "It'll be a wide open race."

Peppin, the Republican strategist, said the midterms results demonstrated the party needed a new direction. "I sincerely hope that we've turned the page from the Trump era, and that we'll have new players, new issues and a new focus moving forward."

articles.title: Leading ice hockey nations, sponsors oppose Russia's return
articles.summary: Ice hockey's governing body says the impact of a court decision forcing it to reinstate Russia presents "significant practical and sporting challenges." Several leading nations say they won't play…

image.caption: The Court of Arbitration says Russian teams can return to international ice hockey, but against whom? And where?Image: Maksim Konstantinov/Imago Images

blocks.text: The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) said in a statement on Wednesday that the impact of last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) decision requiring it to reinstate Russia to international play had been "significantly underestimated."

It added that it "maintains" its disagreement with the decision and that it remained "in dialogue with Member National Associations, organizing committees, host authorities and other key stakeholders to determine the best way forward."

Shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the IIHF barred its teams from competing in international ice hockey tournaments, citing security concerns. In last Friday's ruling, the CAS said that the IIHF's concerns were "not supported by sufficient evidence."

Wednesday's statement comes after two days of talks by the IIHF Council aimed at charting a way forward following Friday's CAS decision, which appears to have caught most of the international ice hockey community off guard.

Two of the organizing committees the statement refers to are those of Canada, which is due to host the IIHF World Junior Championship starting next month, and Germany, which is to host the IIHF Men's World Championship next May. Both countries are strong supporters of Ukraine in its war against Russia, and both have expressed serious reservations about their upcoming tournaments in light of the CAS ruling.
'Russians will not be in Canada'
On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ruled out allowing Russians to compete in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he told reporters at a press conference in Antigua, where he was attending a Commonwealth meeting.
"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

blocks.caption: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has ruled out Russian participation in the World Junior Ice Hockey Tournament in Alberta next monthImage: Jon Blacker/The Canadian Press/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last weekend, Frank Lutz, chairman of the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) conceded in a television interview that following the CAS decision, the DEB would "also have to consider the option of handing back (hosting rights to) this championship."
Lutz was to discuss the matter with government officials in Berlin this week. A government spokesman said on the weekend that Berlin "takes a very critical view" of the ruling.
Growing European boycott of Russia
Meanwhile, the ice hockey association of Finland, the defending men's world champions, has been spearheading an effort to boycott upcoming IIHF tournaments should the Russians be allowed to compete.

"We are currently working to bring as many countries as possible into a united front to tell the IIHF that none of us will play against Russia under these circumstances," Finnish Ice Hockey Association boss Heikki Hietanen said in a statement released on the organization's website on Monday.
"Our stance is that we will not play against Russia as long as the war of aggression against Ukraine continues," added Hietanen, who is also a member of the IIHF Council.
Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Czechia have since made similar statements.
"The Three Crowns will not play Russia in coming world championship tournaments," Swedish Ice Hockey Federation boss Anders Larsson said.
This came shortly after Norway said it would not play Russia at the Men's World Championship and the Danish Ice Hockey Federation issued a similar statement on its website.

"Denmark will – based on the current situation and the information available to us today – not play against Russia at the World Championship in Germany in May 2027," it read. Denmark did not qualify for the World Juniors.
Czechia Ice Hockey Association President Alois Hadamczik confirmed on Tuesday that they too would refrain from playing Russian teams.
Latvia's federation said it “reaffirms its longstanding and firm position" not to play against Russia or its ally Belarus.
Alexander Helwig, chairman of the Austrian Ice Hockey Association told public broadcaster ORF that “as of now, we would certainly not play against Russia."
USA Hockey has yet to comment on the CAS ruling.

blocks.caption: The AJ Products and Skoda logos have long been a familiar sight at World Ice Hockey ChampionshipsImage: Richard Wareham/IMAGO

blocks.text: Sponsors having second thoughts

At the same time, sponsors of IIHF tournaments are also getting cold feet. Skoda, which has been the main sponsor of the Men's World Championship for more than three decades, told the Associated Press that it would "reassess" its position if Russia takes part.

"We do not support the Court of Arbitration for Sport's decision regarding the participation of Russian national teams in IIHF competitions. With Russia's aggression continuing, we believe the Russian national team's return to the world championship is incompatible with the values we have consistently upheld," the Czech carmaker said.

Skoda isn't alone either, Finnish tire manufacturer Nokian had said it would end its backing if Russia took part and Swedish furniture maker AJ Products, whose logo has been seen on the boards and officials' jerseys at World Championships since 1989, said Monday it would ask for its logo not to be shown.

With the IIHF Council having failed to agree on how to proceed during its meetings on Monday and Tuesday, President Franz Reindl told Germany's SID news agency on Wednesday, that it would reconvene for further talks on Thursday.

articles.title: French blood banks hacked in latest cyber-attack on Europe
articles.summary: Temperature and defrosting thresholds raised to ‘very high levels’ at three cold stores stocking vital blood products

blocks.text: France’s national blood service has said hackers accessed control systems and boosted temperatures at three cold stores stocking vital blood products, in an apparent escalation of recent cyber-attacks on fridges and freezers across Europe.

The French blood service (EFS) said temperature and defrosting thresholds had been raised to “very high levels” in the attack, adding that its alarm systems had allowed technicians to intervene before the products were compromised.

The EFS is France’s public blood transfusion operator, collecting, testing, preparing and distributing products such as blood, plasma and platelets to more than 1,900 hospitals around the country. It supports more than a million patients a year.

The attack, which EFS said had occurred overnight on Monday, came as the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in supermarkets in almost a dozen European countries soared as high as 50C (122F), causing millions of euros of food damage.

Retailers in Italy, Germany, Romania and the UK were targeted on Tuesday, after Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems the previous day.

In a wave of attacks in France last month, hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets. A regional branch of France’s Crédit Mutuel bank said on Wednesday it had been the victim of a cyber-attack.

Something similar may have happened in the US in early August, when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries in at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack.

After Italy’s government held emergency talks with intelligence officials on Tuesday, Thomas Regnier, an EU spokesperson, said the bloc’s agencies were holding urgent discussions with national authorities to formulate a collective response.

“These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents,” he said, declining to name any potential culprits. No motive for the attacks is known and no one has claimed responsibility.

A growing range of devices, including commercial refrigeration systems, can be monitored and controlled remotely. Without patching to repair emerging vulnerabilities, internet-connected software can leave code open to hackers.
after newsletter promotion

Some authorities and experts fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in the aftermath of Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Western intelligence officials say Moscow is waging a campaign of sabotage in Europe that is taking many forms.

Rafe Pilling, the senior director for threat intelligence at the cybersecurity company Sophos, told the Guardian this week the most plausible attribution scenarios were a “state-based signalling and demonstration of capability” or a lone-wolf hacker.

EFS said it was not directly targeted, with the attacks hitting cold stores run by its contractors. Products stored in the affected rooms, which included plasma bags for transfusions and medicine manufacturing, had been moved to other sites.
It added that France’s national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI) and the health ministry had been alerted, and monitoring of all its equipment had been reinforced.

articles.title: In new memoir, Harper says he offered Carney a job — but not finance minister
articles.summary: Former prime minister Stephen Harper says he offered Mark Carney, then the governor of the Bank of Canada, a role in his Conservative government in 2012 — though not as finance minister. Not right…

image.caption: Former prime minister Stephen Harper, right, and Prime Minister Mark Carney share a laugh during a ceremony for Harper's official portrait unveiling in Ottawa on Feb 3, 2026. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Former prime minister Stephen Harper says he offered Mark Carney, then the governor of the Bank of Canada, a role in his Conservative government in 2012 — though not as finance minister. Not right away, at least.
Harper also writes he wasn't consulted on policy creating 'barbaric cultural practices hotline'
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 04, 2026 8:18 AM EST | Last Updated: 12 minutes ago

In his new book Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister, Harper says he told Carney the finance position was already taken but indicated that he would be next in line for the job when it became vacant.

"Obviously, I did not offer him the post of minister of finance, as it was then not available. However, I indicated that, if he chose to join the government, he would be the leading candidate should the post come open," Harper writes.

Carney said in an interview with CBC News during the 2025 Liberal leadership race that Harper had "asked me if I would be his finance minister in 2012." He said at the time it wouldn't be appropriate to go directly from the Bank of Canada governorship to party politics.
Liberal leadership hopeful Mark Carney on how he'd change Canada's carbon tax

In his book, released Tuesday, Harper says while Carney was "highly effective" as bank governor, his finance minister, Jim Flaherty, was "increasingly" worried in the wake of the 2011 election that Carney was nurturing political ambitions and might wish to seek the Liberal Party leadership — something widely rumoured at the time.
"This was a serious concern for us," Harper writes.

Harper says he brought it up with Nigel Wright, his chief of staff, who suggested a job offer would either secure Carney's services for the government or force him to rule out a Liberal leadership bid, since he was in the non-partisan role of bank governor.
"Mark took some time to reflect on the opportunity, ultimately declaring that he should stay out of partisan politics," he said, noting Carney left soon after for the top job at the Bank of England.

items: Mark Carney says former prime minister Stephen Harper asked him to be finance minister
Former prime minister Harper accuses Carney of overblowing role during financial crisis

blocks.text: The mention of Carney is just a small aside in the nearly 650-page memoir. Harper says he felt he should address the issue since it has "occasionally cropped up in the media."
The book offers Harper's perspective on his tenure in Canadian politics from start to finish, from uniting the right under the modern Conservative party, through a decade in government.
Not consulted on 'barbaric cultural practices hotline'
It also contains a rare first-person account of Harper's final election campaign and the defeat of his government in 2015.
The former prime minister writes that he debated stepping down from the leadership in the summer of 2014 to rejuvenate the party.

Harper says after deciding to remain at the helm and lead his party into what he knew would be a tough race, he decided he would serve until just after the 150th anniversary of Confederation on July 1, 2017, then call a leadership race.

Harper also says he only learned of one of the most controversial episodes of the 2015 election — his party's embrace of a "barbaric cultural practices hotline" — during his preparation for the French leaders' debate in Montreal when the news "flashed across my screen."

The announcement of the proposed tip line — which frustrated red Tories and hindered the party's outreach efforts with multicultural communities years after the fact — was fronted at the time by former cabinet ministers Kellie Leitch and Chris Alexander.
Harper writes he was "furious" upon learning about the policy, which he says he was not consulted on and had to defend on the campaign trail.

The book spans decades of Canadian political history. It includes Harper's description of face-to-face standoffs with Russian President Vladimir Putin at G8 meetings, his reaction to the 2008 parliamentary crisis — when opposition parties attempted and failed to form a coalition government to oust the Conservatives — and Harper's personal experience during the 2014 shooting on Parliament Hill, which happened when he was without his normal personal protective detail.

The former prime minister also offers up occasional reflections on current matters. While he attended the World Economic Forum (WEF) in Davos twice during his time in office, he now says he opposes it.

If he were prime minister today, Harper writes, he would end the Canadian government's participation in the WEF — an event he describes as a once-useful forum that has become a club for advancing the "narrow interests of its globalist, elitist attendees."
