articles.title: No catastrophic financial hit required to fight climate change, scientists say in landmark court case
articles.summary: Canada does not need to shut down its industries or take a catastrophic financial hit to effectively fight climate change, one of the country's leading climate scientists testified during a landmark…

image.caption: A youth climate protest in Vancouver in 2023. This month, a historic youth climate trial has seen leading scientists testify in federal court in Vancouver. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada does not need to shut down its industries or take a catastrophic financial hit to effectively fight climate change, one of the country's leading climate scientists testified during a landmark trial in a Vancouver courtroom this week.

Canada needs to transform its energy system and prepare for a new, low-emissions future, said Simon Donner, a professor at the University of British Columbia who has been a major voice on climate science and policy for years.

"It's going to cost money to change technologies, to transform the way we do some things. But there's also benefits, because that means the new technologies are things that can also make you money," Donner told the court Tuesday.

Donner was testifying as witness for the 15 youth plaintiffs who are suing the federal government, arguing that Ottawa is violating their constitutional rights by not doing enough to reduce carbon emissions and ensure a livable future.
Simon Donner is a leading climate science and public policy researcher at the University of British Columbia. (Don Erhardt)

The government, whose witnesses will testify next week, is expected to argue that Canada's action cannot be sufficiently linked to the climate harms facing the plaintiffs as climate change is a global problem. In their cross-examination of Donner, the government's lawyer asked him if specific carbon molecules in the atmosphere, and therefore specific climate impacts, could be linked back to Canada.
"No one ever thinks about a pollution problem this way," Donner said in response.
"If you have a whole bunch of factories that have pipes dumping mercury into a lake, no one is looking at, 'Did my specific molecule of mercury, is that the one that led to the death of this fish?'"
Are Canada's climate targets changing? Minister says feds are 'stepping up'

Donner's message is familiar — he has been speaking about the need for decarbonization and contributing to international and Canadian climate policy for over a decade — but his courtroom platform is new, reflecting the recent trajectory of climate action under Prime Minister Mark Carney's government.
Feds, climate advisory body at odds
Donner was the co-chair of the Net-Zero Advisory Body, an independent panel of experts established by Justin Trudeau's government in 2022.

The body was supposed to guide the government's climate plan, but in 2025, Donner and Catherine Abreu, another member, publicly quit and said their advice was not being sought or considered by the government as it tried to fast-track approvals for LNG and other fossil fuel and mining projects.

The NZAB is now down to three members, from a potential size of 15, and its work is in "remission" according to Damon Matthews, one of the remaining members and a climate scientist at Concordia University.

items: Can the Carney government's second budget help put Canada on a path to net zero?

blocks.text: Matthews told CBC on Tuesday that the NZAB does not have the resources to fulfill its mandate, and that there has been minimal communication from the government since the last election. Though, he said NZAB is currently in talks with the federal environment minister on a path to revive its work.
Matthews has contributed a report on behalf of a group of youth applicants in another climate lawsuit targeting the Ontario government.
"Maybe the legal system is a way that we can put some brakes on the headwinds that are trying very hard to stall, delay, and prevent climate action in this country," he said.
Can you sue Canada for not doing enough about climate change?
Scientists outline path to lower emissions

Donner has been joined by several prominent Canadian scientists testifying in the Vancouver courtroom on behalf of the youth plaintiffs. The trial is currently in its second week, with witnesses for the plaintiffs testifying.

The government's witnesses, which include experts in climate science, law and economics, will testify from Nov. 9 to Nov. 20. After that, the court will take a pause and return in February, when lawyers for both sides will make their closing statements.

Last week, Kirsten Zickfeld, a professor of climate science at Simon Fraser University, took the witness box to speak about the carbon budget, which is the amount of carbon emissions that can be emitted before global warming reaches unsafe levels.

items: Oil and gas emissions rising as other sectors mostly flat, federal data shows
Is Canada flunking climate? The picture isn’t great, but there might be a way out

blocks.text: Canada, as one of the 10 largest carbon emitters in the world both currently and historically, has already surpassed its fair share of the carbon budget, she testified.

"To stabilize global average temperature, global carbon dioxide emissions need to be reduced to at least net zero and the emission of other greenhouse gases such as methane and nitrous oxide need to be strongly reduced," she said.
In the coming week, University of Ottawa professor Nicholas Rivers, a prominent expert in climate policy and economic modelling, will testify on pathways to achieve lower emissions.
Youth should be 'planning their futures, not fighting in court'

Many of the youth plaintiffs also testified about how climate disasters have affected their lives. Most of them were in their tweens or teens when the case was first filed in 2019; since then they have lived through disasters like the 2023 Yellowknife wildfires, the 2021 B.C. heat dome, major floods, drought and poor air quality from fire smoke.
Donner's testimony focused on research from government reports and climate attribution studies that says such disasters will become more severe and frequent if emissions don't come down.

"These are stories that so many Canadians have either lived firsthand or know people who have been through those types of impacts," said Andrew Gage, staff lawyer at West Coast Environmental Law, which is supporting the case.
Canadian youth launch climate lawsuit against federal government

Tzeporah Berman, a Canadian climate campaigner, says the timing of the trial is remarkable both because climate disasters have become so obvious and frequent — at the same time that the federal government is scaling back action on reducing emissions.

"I've heard a lot of people this week saying they admire [the youth plaintiffs]. We owe our youth more than admiration, we owe them action," said Berman, who chairs the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, which seeks to build global agreement on ending the use of oil, gas and coal.
"These young Canadians should be planning their futures, not fighting in court to protect the possibility of having one."

articles.title: The give and take (and partisan wrangling) in Alberta's urban-rural hybrid riding maps
articles.summary: The last boundary panel's chair urged the new panel not to alter ridings in southern Alberta. They did.

image.caption: Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi flips through the new report of Alberta's electoral boundaries independent advisory panel at a news conference. (CBC)

blocks.text: When the judge who led Alberta’s boundaries commission gave politicians a narrow path to revise his panel’s work and rescue two rural ridings from the chopping block, Justice Dallas Miller added a few provisos to protect his electoral map work.

The first condition, which the Smith government adopted, stated that “restoration of the two electoral divisions should: have no impact on any electoral division in Airdrie or containing territory south of Airdrie’s southernmost border…”
And lo and behold, where has the new boundary panel done its most controversial redrawing?
In Lethbridge, Calgary and Canmore. All south of Airdrie.
NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi has called it a “Trump-style, MAGA gerrymandered map” that safeguards UCP-held territory in southern Alberta. Adopt it, Nenshi has warned, and “we’ll see them in court.”
Premier Danielle Smith has expressed early favour for the new plan, regardless of its apparent overstepping of the conditions her side set on her new boundary advisory group.

Back in April, when United Conservatives shelved the official commission’s work, she had insisted she was accepting that majority report, just with Justice Dallas Miller’s extra recommendations which proposed modest tweaks.
"You'll see that in his Recommendation Five, he is quite prescriptive about the areas that he thinks are problematic," she told reporters.

The new panel chaired by retired judge Brian O’Ferrall, however, did not feel so fettered about sticking to the confines of what Miller and Alberta’s legislature had set out, stating in its “majority” report that the words in Miller’s fifth recommendation don’t warrant “deification.”
“It was not the ‘Fifth Commandment,’” the report states. “It was simply a bit of political ‘give and take.’”
So what did O’Ferrall’s panel give and take?

It took Lethbridge’s two urban seats and split one of them across three rural ridings that variously stretch up to 150 kilometres in each direction to the U.S. border, the TransCanada Highway, Waterton Lakes National Park and the hamlet of Manyberries, due south of Medicine Hat.
A map showing a sole Lethbridge urban seat, as well as three hybrid electoral divisions combining parts of the city with vast surrounding rural regions. (Advisory panel on electoral boundaries)

It took rural acreage communities from the formerly proposed Cochrane-Springbank riding and dispersed them among three west Calgary districts — which, Nenshi argued, gives thousands of Conservative voters to seats currently held by a trio of UCP cabinet ministers.

It took the Diamond Valley and Longview areas away from adjoining rural ridings south of Calgary and gave them to the Canmore-Banff riding on the other side of Kananaskis Country and a highway partially closed for six months every year.

Not only had Miller, the original commission’s chair, recommended against such tinkering in service of restoring a pair of rural ridings in northern and central Alberta; it’s also not clear that these southern Alberta modifications were even necessary to accommodate the un-eliminating of those two districts.
They weren’t knock-on effects caused by bringing back the riding in Rocky Mountain House and Sundre.
In the case of Springbank and Bearspaw, it was a straightforward bit of subtraction, division and addition, separate from any map work to the north.

According to population figures in the new report, Cochrane’s riding shed 9,703 people, and that same amount was split among the three Calgary ridings, without any corresponding adjustments to any other Calgary constituencies.

It leaves the redesigned Cochrane with 46,785 residents, and 13 per cent below the provincial average riding population. The redrawn Calgary-West-Springbank and Calgary-Bow-Springbank each have more than 58,000 people, nine per cent higher than average.

“Adding Springbank to Calgary Bow is said to potentially favour the party in power,” O’Ferrall’s report acknowledged. “But whether that potential will manifest itself in the next election, not even the pollsters with their voter transpositioning software know for sure.”
Springbank was moved because O’Ferrall and the panel’s UCP appointees felt that rural area had more connection to Calgary than to the small town of Cochrane to its north.

Similarly, it felt that “Lethbridge is not an isolated urban municipality,” but is the hub of southern Alberta’s agri-business, health and service district. Therefore, it partially becomes three hub-and-spoke ridings that nearly stretch from Saskatchewan to British Columbia — and, the NDP argues, erases one of Lethbridge’s politically competitive ridings and dilutes those votes in UCP-friendly zones.
LISTEN | Alberta @ Noon on the boundary revisions:
Alberta at Noon52:39Redrawing Alberta's electoral boundaries
O’Farrell and his UCP-appointed majority dismiss complaints their work is unconstitutional as “polarizing nonsense.”

They take similar umbrage in their report with the NDP-appointed minority’s protests about the new map work in southern Alberta, saying “it can be summarized quite simply. Our proposals are constitutional; yours are not. Our proposals are non-partisan; yours are not.”

For the record, Smith’s cabinet chose O’Ferrall, a former Court of Appeal judge who has donated thousands of dollars to the UCP and federal conservatives since he retired in 2022, and served in court as lawyer for an Alberta Progressive Conservative riding association two decades ago before he was a judge.

The United Conservatives’ two appointees to the panel are Monte Solberg, a former Conservative MP and head of a Calgary-based lobby firm who has donated $2,883 to Smith’s party this year, including some while serving on the panel; and Darwin Durnie, a longtime conservative political donor and municipal public works official who has a lengthy history as a boundary-making hobbyist of sorts, having submitted maps to Alberta’s boundary commissions that propose several rural-urban hybrid ridings.

The NDP’s appointees, constitutional law professor Gerard Kennedy and former Okotoks councillor Brent Robinson, have no record of provincial donations in Elections Alberta’s database. Kennedy has donated federally, predominantly to Conservatives and some to Liberals.
Regardless of how partisan the boundary panelists are or aren’t, the partisan MLAs are set to debate the contentious report in coming days.
Smith likes the idea of Lethbridge’s hybrid ridings, similar to how Medicine Hat is divided between her Brooks-Medicine Hat seat and a UCP colleague’s Cypress-Medicine Hat.

“I represent a hybrid riding, and I think Medicine Hat is well-served by having two representatives. I think Lethbridge will be very well-served by having four representatives,” she told reporters Tuesday.

Premier Danielle Smith, who represents a rural-urban hybrid riding in Medicine Hat, said Lethbridge would be well-served by having several rural-urban hybrid MLAs instead of two city-only MLAs. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

The NDP cannot launch a lawsuit against this new riding map until the legislature approves it and puts it into effect. A successful challenge would have to argue that the ridings violate the “effective representation” guarantees in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms — such a claim could theoretically come from a political party, or the affected residents in Lethbridge or elsewhere, including the few thousand people in Springbank and Bearspaw who find themselves mixed into 50,000-person-plus seats in Alberta’s biggest city.

Original commission chair Miller, for his part, wrote in his report that he didn’t find Lethbridge or Springbank hybrids “necessarily unreasonable or procedurally unfair,” noting that some public members proposed them to the commission. But that report blurb wasn’t part of the government motion that created the do-over boundary review, unlike the one urging against any redrawing work south of Airdrie.

Smith discussed on Tuesday being ready to “assemble a legal team” ahead of a potential court challenge. When asked about Miller’s warning on southern ridings she said: “I'll take a closer look at it and talk to the lawyers about that.”

articles.title: A runner died in the New York City Marathon. Have the risks changed as more people race?
articles.summary: Every year, amid our current running boom, more and more people vie for the chance to lace up their sneakers and push themselves 42.2 kilometres to cross that finish line. But every year, young and…

image.caption: Runners cross the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge during the New York City Marathon on Sunday. Rachel Apa died only a few kilometres from the finish. (Heather Khalifa/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Every year, amid our current running boom, more and more people vie for the chance to lace up their sneakers and push themselves 42.2 kilometres to cross that finish line. But every year, young and seemingly healthy people also die trying.
Rachel Apa, 24, died after collapsing just over 3 km from the finish line
She was just a few kilometres from the finish line.
A record-breaking 61,146 runners completed the New York City Marathon on Sunday. But Rachel Apa, despite being in what her father describes as perfect health, wasn't one of them.

The 24-year-old athlete collapsed near mile 24, or about 38.6 kilometres into the 42.2-kilometre race. Despite the life-saving efforts of bystanders, paramedics and then hospital doctors, she was pronounced dead later that night, her grieving parents told the New York Times.
"It's unfathomable," her father Steve Apa, who could not be reached by CBC News, told the news outlet.

Every year, more and more people vie for the chance to lace up their sneakers and push themselves 42.2 kilometres to cross that finish line. But every year, young and seemingly healthy people also die trying — typically of heart failure or cardiac arrest.

All told, including Rachel Apa, at least six runners have died racing in marathons and half-marathons around the world in the past six months alone. Still, experts say the incidence rate is very low, given that millions of people run them every year.

Marathons aren't any riskier than they were 20 years ago, but they are far more popular, explained Jack Goodman, a professor emeritus in kinesiology at the University of Toronto, and adjunct scientist of cardiovascular research at Toronto's University Health Network.
"When the population is so large, there are bound to be more cases, rare as they are," Goodman told CBC News.

Any time you have thousands of people in the same space, based on probabilities, one of them will have a cardiac event, Dr. Christopher Labos, a cardiologist and epidemiologist in Montreal, told CBC News.
"You just hear about it more in the news because it's so shocking when something unexpected like this happens."
Rachel Apa is pictured in the 2023 field hockey roster on the athletics website for Bucknell University in Lewisburg, Pa. (Bucknellbison.com)
Risk of dying has decreased: study

Anyone who has tried to register for a marathon in the last few years can tell you how popular they've become. A record 1.3 million people have already applied to run the 2027 London Marathon. So many people have tried to register for the Boston Marathon in recent years that they've tightened their qualifying times.

In the U.S. alone, more than 29 million people completed marathons and half-marathons in between 2010 and 2023, notes a 2025 study published the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA). That's triple the number compared to a decade earlier, the authors add.

items: 70-year-old Ottawa woman sets new marathon world record
More kids are running marathons. A teen's death reignites a debate about the risks

blocks.text: Overall, the risk of risk of death is about one in 150,000 runners, notes a 2019 global review in the BMJ medical journal. Typically, the risk is much higher for men, the cause is often coronary artery disease and the deaths most often occur in the last quarter of the race, the study says.
"There are infrequent deaths, which are often reported widely, and may create unnecessary alarm about the potential risks," the authors wrote.

The 2025 JAMA study points out that the risk of dying from a cardiac event during long-distance running races in the U.S. has actually gone down by about 50 per cent in recent years — likely due to more effective emergency planning, including access to defibrillators.

But the study also noted a small uptick in non-fatal cardiac events since 2020, which the authors hypothesized could be due to less access to health care during the COVID-19 pandemic, leading to reduced detection of cardiovascular disease.
Runners make their way through Queens during the New York City Marathon Sunday. (Heather Khalifa/The Associated Press)
Usually a pre-existing cause, expert says
Most often, in the case of death, there's underlying coronary disease the runner didn't know about and never caused them a problem until the race, said Goodman.
"Sudden cardiac death is, unfortunately, not a terribly uncommon first symptom of heart disease," he said.

Just last month, 24-year-old Treyton Lara collapsed at mile 20 of the Portland Marathon and died. He'd experienced a sudden cardiac arrest, his family said. In January, Julien Autissier, 33, collapsed around the 19-mile mark of the Miami marathon and died in the hospital. Doctors also suspected sudden cardiac arrest, according to the Miami New Times.

Roland Liinar, 25, died last May after collapsing in the Rimi Riga Marathon in Latvia. The same month, two other runners died after collapsing while competing in half-marathons in New York and the U.K.

Still, from a public health perspective, the problem most people have is moving too little, not moving too much, said Lagos, the cardiologist and epidemiologist. And if you're a young healthy person who trained properly for a marathon, a cardiac event is "almost certainly not going to happen in your case."
Runners cross the finish line in Central Park on Sunday. (Angelina Katsanis/The Associated Press)
'She did everything she's supposed to'

Apa, an industrial-technology product manager, had run to raise money for Parkinson's disease in honour of her grandfather. On her fundraiser page, which had raised more than $26,000 US by Tuesday evening, Apa called him her "role model."

New York Road Runners, the non-profit club that stages the New York City Marathon, said in a news release that CPR was administered to Apa by a bystander and later by event medical staff. A defibrillator was also used before paramedics took Apa to the Mount Sinai Hospital, reports The Associated Press.
The former Division I field hockey player at Bucknell University was in critical condition when she was brought to the hospital, where doctors unsuccessfully tried to save her for several hours.

items: A workout class sent this St. John's woman to hospital. She's not the only one
'Extreme' workouts drive spike in 'rhabdo' cases among young N.L. women, says doctor

blocks.text: Steve Apa says Rachel's cause of death Sunday was rhabdomyolysis, a rare but serious condition where the muscle cells break down and leak into the bloodstream. Rhabdo, as it is often called, can be brought on by severe physical exertion.

Exercise-induced rhabdo cases aren't tracked across Canada, CBC News has previously reported. But there was recently a spike of cases in young women in St. John's, with health officials pointing to intense workouts and social media competitiveness.
It was her first marathon, but Rachel was a lifelong athlete, her father told USA Today, and she had trained carefully for months.
"She did everything she's supposed to."
Dangerous fitness: What is rhabdomyolysis?
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Clarington's new mayor will serve with a councillor charged for allegedly threatening him
articles.summary: The incoming mayor of Clarington, Ont., will take office alongside a councillor who has been criminally charged with uttering threats against him, raising questions about how council will navigate…

image.caption: Coun. Corinna Trail, left, was charged in December with two counts of uttering threats over a voicemail to Tom Dingwall. The allegations against her have not been proven in court. (Corinnatraill.ca/Tomdingwall.ca)

blocks.text: Toronto

The incoming mayor of Clarington, Ont., will take office alongside a councillor who has been criminally charged with uttering threats against him, raising questions about how council will navigate the matter.
Coun. Corinna Traill was charged in December with 2 counts of uttering threats
Coun. Corinna Traill was charged in December with two counts of uttering threats in a voicemail she allegedly left Tom Dingwall. The allegations against her have not been proven in court.
Traill was re-elected this month as councillor for Ward 3, and will serve her fifth term. Dingwall was elected mayor, defeating incumbent Mayor Adrian Foster, who has held office since 2010.

John Mascarin, a lawyer with Aird & Berlis LLP who specializes in municipal law, says he’s not aware of a situation like this, where criminal proceedings are underway involving multiple members of council.

"You're going into a council where you know you have some dysfunction even before it starts,” Mascarin said. “That's going to be tough for the council to oversee that and I'm not really sure how they're going to manage it."

John Mascarin, a lawyer with Aird & Berlis LLP who specializes in municipal law, said he thinks it will be hard to navigate what he said may be 'a very strained relationship' between Dingwall and Traill. (Aird Berlis)
Traill previously denied making the threats, saying the voicemail in question was created using artificial intelligence.
She declined an interview but said in an emailed statement that she was grateful for the “tremendous and continued support” from her ward.

items: Clarington councillor charged with uttering threats

blocks.text: “It will be my pleasure to work with Mayor Elect Tom Dingwall, and I would like to again extend my congratulations on his victory,” she said in a statement.
Dingwall did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
CBC News asked Traill, her legal counsel and Dingwall for the status of the court case, but didn’t get a response.
Melissa Westover, spokesperson for the Municipality of Clarington, declined to comment, saying any questions about the incoming council should be directed to the councillors.
Dingwall said voicemail included sexual assault threat

In a social media post in September that now appears to be deleted, Dingwall said he received a voicemail from Traill in August, telling him to stay out of next year’s mayoral race to allow a friend of hers to “run unencumbered.”
Dingwall went on to say that the message "made it clear" that if he did not, he would be killed and his wife would be sexually assaulted.

Coun. Granville Anderson, who was re-elected to his position as regional councillor for Ward 1 and Ward 2, said he hopes that all council members will focus on prioritizing residents’ needs during this upcoming term. (Granvilleanderson.ca)
Coun. Granville Anderson, who was re-elected to his position as regional councillor for Ward 1 and Ward 2, said the criminal matter is “not a good look for Clarington.”
He said doesn’t know Dingwall well, but hopes that all council members will focus on prioritizing residents’ needs during the upcoming term.
“I hope he’ll come in and put the interests of Clarington residents first, and we can work together to build this community up,” he said.
But Mascarin said he thinks it will be hard to navigate what he said may be “a very strained relationship” between Dingwall and Traill.
He said mayors have always had the role of trying to bring council together and encourage collaborative work – but this role may be fraught considering the ongoing criminal matter.
“It’s going to be a very tricky situation for this council,” he said.
CBC News reached out to all other members of council for the upcoming term but didn’t receive a response.
What happens if Traill is found guilty?
If Traill is found guilty, Mascarin said a conviction alone wouldn’t mean she’s automatically removed from office.
However, if she were incarcerated, she would be automatically disqualified from holding office, he said.

Ontario's Municipal Accountability Act, Bill 9, also allows a councillor to be removed from their seat for a serious violation of the province’s standardized code of conduct for municipal officials. While the bill has passed, it hasn’t yet been proclaimed into force Mascarin said.
New law will hold city politicians accountable

Mascarin said the process could include an investigation by the municipality's integrity commissioner and the provincial integrity commissioner. Such investigations can only begin after a criminal matter has concluded, he said.

items: Tito-Dante Marimpietri elected Oshawa’s next mayor as polls show incumbents re-elected in Pickering, Whitby

blocks.text: Ultimately, council has to vote unanimously to remove a member, which Mascarin said he thinks would be a rare occurrence.
“I’ve often said that you’re just not going to find that [unanimity], especially on something that’s quasi-controversial,” he said.
Anderson declined to comment on what may happen if Traill is found guilty.
“We will cross that bridge, if that should happen,” he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Rochelle Raveendran is a reporter for CBC News in Oshawa. She can be reached at: rochelle.raveendran@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Miliband criticises Blair’s slavery statement and defends Burnham’s plan for proper apology – UK politics live
articles.summary:
The foreign secretary added that the UK will not shift its position on reparations

Good morning. Wednesdays are normally the most exciting day of the week at Westminster, because it’s PMQs,…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 2m agoBurnham says Commonwealth 'more important today than ever before'

blocks.text: Burnham says Commonwealth 'more important today than ever before'

Andy Burnham has described the Commonwealth as “more important today than ever before” amid “such volatile times”. He used the phrase in a meeting with his Antigua and Barbuda counterpart Gaston Browne, who is hosting the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm).
In a readout of the meeting, released this morning, a No 10 spokesperson said:

double quotation markThe prime minister thanked Prime Minister Browne for the warm welcome from Antigua and Barbuda and for hosting Commonwealth leaders at such an important time. In such volatile times, it was clear that the Commonwealth was more important today than ever before, the prime minister added.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham (right) with Gaston Browne  ahead of a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Chogm. Photograph: Kin Cheung/PA

blocks.text: Good morning. Wednesdays are normally the most exciting day of the week at Westminster, because it’s PMQs, but today (unless we get some mega surprise) all the action is taking place somewhere else. In part, that’s because Andy Burnham is still at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. But mostly because anyone in SW1 with even a passing interest in politics will be far more interested in the outcome of the US midterm elections. You can catch up with all the drama on our US politics live blog.

While the US results are undoubtedly fascinating, quite how relevant they are to the UK is a bit harder to discern. Donald Trump is still president for the next two years, and none of the chaos he has caused for Britain and other European allies is going to go away; conceivably, he could end up even more disruptive. Trump was first elected president in 2016 only months after the UK voted for Brexit and there will be progressives in Britain hoping the US results show that what Ed Davey is this morning calling the “politics of hate, division and economic harm” might be on their way out this side of the pond too. Maybe? But it is probably too soon to get carried away. Our US coverage is all here. In so far as there is any interesting UK reaction, I will post it here.

Back to the Commonwealth summit, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has given an interview to the BBC in which he defended Burnham’s decision to open talks about a proper UK apology for slavery. In particular, Miliband was critical of Tony Blair’s attempts to settle this issue with what Miliband described as a “sorry not sorry” apology.

Miliband was referring to this statement that Blair issued in 2006, written up at the time by the Guardian here. Blair said the slave trade was “profoundly shameful” and he expressed “deep sorrow that it ever happened”. But he did not formally apologise.
In an interview with the BBC’s Newscast podcast, Miliband said Burnham wanted a different approach. He said:

double quotation markPeople have been honestly a bit bruised by the past, what happened in the past, the sense that we just really just wanted to sweep this issue under the carpet and not confront it. My sense is there’s a bit of a sigh of relief that, OK … at least there’s a sense of we’ve got a shared interest now in moving the Commonwealth on.
Miliband said Blair “did sort of do a kind of sorry not sorry situation”. He added: “He kind of expressed ‘sorrow, but’ and then said sorry, and then it was walked back by No 10.”

(Miliband has for many years had a strained relationship with the former prime minister, who was opposed to the way Miliband criticised some aspects of New Labour’s record when he was party leader between 2010 and 2015. These latest remarks are just the latest example of feuding between the two of them.)

Burnham has said he wants a “structured dialogue” with Commonwealth countries about the wording of an apology. Asked whether the government might reach the point of a formal apology by the time it hosts the G20 leaders’ summit in Manchester next November, Miliband said: “Broadly speaking, yes.”
But he also stressed that the UK was not offering reparations. Asked whether the government’s new approach could end up costing UK taxpayers a penny more, Miliband replied:

double quotation markNo … For us, that’s never been what it’s about. And that’s why it’s been important that … I did have this conversation with our partners in advance. I said, ‘Look, we are going to say we are willing to say that we’re open to an apology, but we’re not going to shift our position on reparations.’ It’s not for us. It’s not the right answer. It’s not practical. It’s not feasible for us, but there are things we can work on co-operatively.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, gives evidence to the Commons health committee.
10am: Lucy Powell, the education secretary, gives evidence to the Commons education committee.
Noon: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, faces Alex Burghart, the deputy Conservative leader, at PMQs.
Afternoon (UK time): Andy Burnham is due to record a pooled TV interview while attending the final day of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.
2.15pm: Jonathan Haskel, chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, gives evidence with colleagues to the Commons Treasury committee about the budget.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: In new study, think tank raises several red flags over expanded oil exploration in Palawan
articles.summary: Palawan"s marine biodiversity and food system are at risk amid expanded oil exploration around the island, according to a new study published by non-government organization Center for Energy,…

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 4:54pm

Palawan’s marine biodiversity and food system are at risk amid expanded oil exploration around the island, according to a new study published by non-government organization Center for Energy, Ecology, and Development (CEED).

The scoping paper titled “Don’t Drill Paradise,” authored by researcher Charlene Jemima Lopez, analyzed the government’s different national policies and agreements on fuel, and utilized different case studies to show the impacts of oil exploration.

“Despite the province’s ecological and environmental importance, upstream exploration and production activities are concentrated in Palawan. It hosts 14 active offshore petroleum service contracts, with several additional applications pending in nearby areas,” the study found.

CEED raised several risks to the environment when it came to expanded oil exploration, including seismic airguns that caused harmful noise to marine life, as well as the drilling of wells that damage the seabed.
Methane, a principal component of fossil gas and a potent greenhouse gas, contributed significantly to near-total global warming. This methane could escape through equipment leaks, venting, and more.

Coastal communities are also directly impacted by these upstream activities, with fisherfolk reporting lower catches. Every stage of gas projects posed a risk of oil contamination which could devastate the marine ecosystem, leading to fishing bans and the closure of tourism industries.
Government policies also tended to favor large conglomerates, offering little protection for host communities.

“The law provides no clear mechanism for reparations for damages suffered by communities or the environment. It merely requires contractors to give priority in employment to qualified local residents, effectively reducing host communities to a source of labor, while any direct community benefits remain discretionary and dependent on negotiations between the national government and the contractor,” the study read.
The study also raised alarm over the environmental damage to the food system in Palawan.
Since Palawan fisheries are already under pressure from overfishing, upstream oil activities could make it further vulnerable.

“Reduced fish catch would not only undermine the incomes of fishing communities but constrain the availability and affordability of fish as a source of food–resulting in higher prices that could affect the whole country,” the study found.
Based on its findings, the study concluded that the Marcos administration has delayed the country’s transition into using renewable energy,

“The current policy directions of the Marcos administration places communities and marine life at risk while delaying, rather than facilitating, the transition to renewable energy. Gas exploration and production disrupts marine ecosystems even before gas reserves are discovered. At the same time, large investments in the fossil gas industry divert resources away from renewable energy and lock the country into prolonged fossil-fuel dependence,” the study read.

In 2022, Marcos called fossil gas as an interim fuel while the country transitioned into renewable energy. Liquified natural gas (LNG) was also considered a necessary transition fuel under the Philippine Energy Plan.
Despite this, CEED said there was a “gas boom” under the Marcos administration. Before the Marcos admin, there were only 10 petroleum service contracts (PSC).
Twelve new PSC’s were awarded during his term, raising the country’s contracts to 22.

“If gas truly is a ‘transition fuel’, fossil gas should be phased out after displacing coal and oil in the energy mix. Yet, until now, there is no oil and coal phase-out and neither is there any plan to phase out gas after it has supposedly acted as a transition fuel,” the research said.

The Marcos admin has been urged to phase out fossil fuels and to halt the development of gas fields and awarding of PSCs. The study also recommended strengthening environmental and social safeguards for oil and gas activities.
The CEED also urged the local government of Palawan to reject new development of gas projects and to invest in renewable energy solutions.
Stakeholders are also urged to participate in consultations and demand transparency.
GMA News has reached out to the Department of Energy and the Palace for response to these findings. — LA, GMA News

articles.title: SC amends e-rules for child witnesses; allows video conference, recorded interviews
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has approved the use of video conferencing and other means of technology to protect children if they need to recount traumatic experiences.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 4:47pm
The Supreme Court (SC) has approved the use of video conferencing and other means of technology to protect children if they need to recount traumatic experiences.
In a news release on Wednesday, the SC approved the Revised Rule on the Examination of Child Witnesses (RRECW), which updated how children are questioned in court.

“Key changes include the use of videoconferencing, recorded depositions, recorded interviews, and technological tools to help children explain what happened. These technological tools are in addition to existing testimonial aids such as dolls, drawings, and puppets,” the SC said in a statement.
“Courts may allow children to testify via videoconferencing from outside the courtroom if testifying in person is likely to cause them trauma,” the high court added.
Apart from this, the court may also limit who the child can see and hear, including the accused. However, the accused’s right to confront the witness remains preserved.
Should the child need to identify the accused, the accused may briefly turn on the camera. The child may identify the accused from an image displayed on a screen.

“If a child cannot testify at trial or via videoconferencing due to a disability, health concerns, or other reasons, the child’s testimony may be taken through an electronically recorded deposition in the presence of the judge and lawyers for both sides. The recording may be used in place of the child’s in-court testimony,” the SC said.

Children also cannot be forced to appear and court and must not be present if sexually explicit materials are shown. Records about children are confidential, and anyone found posting them may be held in contempt by the court.
The RRECW also encourages and allows a recorded interview with the child, which will be conducted by a team of professionals.
The recording or the transcript may be presented as evidence, as long as the interviewer asked neutral, open-ended, age-appropriate, and trauma-informed questions without suggesting answers.
The new set of rules applies to children who are victims of crimes, children in conflict with the law, and child witnesses in all cases. —Jean Mangaluz/RF, GMA News

articles.title: [In This Economy] Pax Silica: What’s the Philippines’ trump card?
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump’s visit to the Philippines this month gives President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. a good occasion to explain what we’re negotiating for on Pax Silica

blocks.text: In case you missed it, US President Donald Trump is soon coming to the Philippines. Malacañang has confirmed his attendance at the ASEAN Summit and related meetings in Manila on November 16 to 18.

One deal that Philippine officials had hoped to sign around the time of his visit is the framework for the proposed Pax Silica industrial hub in New Clark City. But as of Tuesday November 3, Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) chief Joshua Bingcang said the framework had been submitted to Malacañang and there was still no signing date. Whether there will be a signing during the visit, and whether Trump himself will sign, remains open.

But in fact, the Philippines already joined Pax Silica in April when it signed the declaration. That brought us into a US-led effort to build more secure supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors, and other technologies that underpin artificial intelligence. The framework now awaiting signature concerns how the proposed 4,000-acre hub in Tarlac would be developed.
Even after that agreement is signed, we’ll still have to see which companies actually invest, what they build, and what they commit to doing here.
The signing date has gotten a lot of attention. But in this piece, I’d like to explore exactly what the Marcos administration is asking for in return. What’s in it for us?
Two recent papers by my UP School of Economics (UPSE) colleague Annette Balaoing-Pelkmans help explain what’s at stake.
In her paper for the UP Center for Integrative and Development Studies (UP CIDS), she draws a distinction between hosting an industry and acquiring the capabilities to do more valuable work in it.

Take semiconductors. Say a multinational opens a plant in Clark and hires Filipino engineers to run equipment that tests chips. Over time, those engineers get better at their jobs: they can test more chips in a day, catch defects earlier, and waste fewer materials.

All of that is valuable, for sure. But imagine that the Filipino team also gets to develop the tests, figure out why the chips are failing, and work with the design team to fix the problem. That’s a different kind of gain. The engineers can take on more complex work, and those skills can travel to other firms or help start new ones. That would be a genuine technology transfer.

You see, the Philippines already assembles and tests semiconductors. The question is how much more of the engineering we’ll get to do. Any foreign company can set up shop in Tarlac and still have its tests designed abroad, buy most of its sophisticated inputs from its usual suppliers, and keep its research at headquarters. Its factory can create jobs and boost exports while leaving our place in the supply chain largely where it was.

Annette’s other paper, a UPSE Discussion Paper, is written from the perspective of the Tatak Pinoy Strategy, helps explain why that can happen. Drawing on consultations in electronics, semiconductors, and IT and business process management, she points to capabilities we already have in areas like chip design and cybersecurity.

The difficulty, she says, is getting more firms and workers to build on them. Take for instance the case of MYPAD, an effort to strengthen microelectronics education and connect it with industry. It lost momentum for lack of sustained institutional backing.
It takes years to train engineers, develop suppliers, and build research partnerships. The institutions doing that work need funding and a clear mandate well after the launch event is over.
There’s another important question to ask: How much of the investment would have happened anyway?

Suppose a company was already looking to expand its Philippine operations. If the government offers it a tax break to move that expansion to Clark, officials might count the entire factory as a win for Pax Silica.

For taxpayers, the relevant gain is whatever the offer actually secured beyond the company’s original plans. Perhaps the firm adds an engineering team, or gives local suppliers a route to qualify for contracts. We should be able to say what that extra benefit is and how much we paid for it.

The same scrutiny should apply to what we build with public money in support of Pax Silica. A more reliable power grid and better freight links can serve many businesses, whether or not the hub attracts its intended tenants.

Infrastructure built for a single investor is a different proposition. Who pays if that investor backs out? And before committing land and water to a project, what will be left for nearby communities and farms in a dry year? Those questions deserve answers while we still have leverage to change the terms.

As Trump’s arrival approaches, let us demand answers to the following questions: Exactly how many Filipinos will be trained and given responsibility for advanced engineering work? Will local firms get a chance to qualify as suppliers, and who will help them meet the standards? If public money goes into joint research, what rights will Philippine universities and firms have to use the results? And what happens to the incentives if the investor falls short?

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] Risks of Pax Silica

blocks.text: In the end, Trump’s visit gives President Marcos a good occasion to explain what we’re negotiating for. He can start by making the proposed terms public and telling us what Filipinos are being asked to put up for the project.

Perhaps Marcos should take a leaf from Trump’s own book. In The Art of the Deal, Trump and his coauthor Tony Schwartz write, “The worst thing you can possibly do in a deal is seem desperate to make it.”

Honestly, I’m no Trump fan, but that’s actually good advice worth taking. Marcos has no reason to treat Pax Silica as our last chance to upgrade Philippine manufacturing. If the terms still need work when Trump comes to Manila, the deal can wait.

The US wants more secure supply chains, and we can offer a site in Clark and decades of experience in semiconductor assembly and testing. In return, though, Marcos should ask for specific commitments on what engineering work will be done here and how Filipino firms can qualify for supplier contracts.
We have a trump card—and we should use it. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Romualdez bid to stop Ombudsman probe
articles.summary: In a statement on Wednesday, November 4, the high court ruled that Romualdez’s petition for certiorari has become moot following the formal filing of criminal charges against him before the…

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 4:43pm
The logo of the Supreme Court at the Supreme Court Building in Manila.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court (SC) has dismissed the petition of detained former House Speaker Martin Romualdez challenging the preliminary investigation conducted by the Office of the Ombudsman over his plunder charge.

In a statement on Wednesday, November 4, the high court ruled that Romualdez’s petition for certiorari had become moot following the formal filing of criminal charges against him before the Sandiganbayan.

Romualdez challenged the preliminary investigation conducted by the Ombudsman, raising objections to the anti-graft body's application for a preliminary hold departure order and a freeze order against him, as well as the alleged inclusion of inadmissible evidence. Romualdez filed the petition on July 31.

The high tribunal also denied the lawmaker's prayer for a temporary restraining order and a writ of preliminary injunction, which aimed to halt the Ombudsman from proceeding with the preliminary investigation.

“The SC ruled that the petition has become moot, or no longer needs to be resolved, because a plunder charge had already been filed against Romualdez before the Sandiganbayan, where he was arraigned and pleaded not guilty,” the Supreme Court’s statement read.
“The SC also found no exceptional circumstances that would justify resolving the petition despite its having become moot,” it added.
Philstar.com has reached out to the Office of the Ombudsman for comment, but it has yet to reply.
Romualdez is currently detained at the Quezon City Jail in Payatas over a non-bailable plunder charge involving P7.44 billion linked to flood control projects.

articles.title: Supreme Court finds Martin Romualdez's bid to halt Ombudsman's probe moot
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has junked the bid of former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez to stop the Ombudsman"s preliminary investigation against him for being moot.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 4:39pm

The Supreme Court (SC) has junked the bid of former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez to stop the Ombudsman’s preliminary investigation against him for being moot, or no longer needs to be resolved.

The High Tribunal made the ruling on Tuesday, November 4, with Romualdez already facing a P7.4 billion plunder charge alongside former House appropriations panel chairperson Zaldy Co of Ako Bicol party-list, his personal assistant Joselyn Tragua Sereño, and Felicito Cristobal Guevarra, president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation.
The charge is in connection with alleged kickbacks from government infrastructure projects particularly those on flood control.

"The SC dismissed the petition for certiorari filed by Rep. Ferdinand Martin Romualdez challenging the preliminary investigation conducted by the respondent Office of the Ombudsman, including its application for a preliminary hold departure order and freeze order against him and the alleged use of inadmissible evidence," the SC said.
"The SC also denied Romualdez's prayer for a temporary restraining order and/or a writ of preliminary injunction to stop the respondent from continuing the preliminary investigation," it added.

"The SC ruled that the petition has become moot, or no longer needs to be resolved, because a plunder charge had already been filed against Romualdez before the Sandiganbayan, where he was arraigned and pleaded not guilty,” the High Tribunal said.
The SC said there are no “exceptional circumstances” that would justify resolving the petition despite its having become moot.
Romualdez, who is detained in New Quezon City jail in Payatas, has since filed a petition for bail to secure temporary liberty amid a plunder case leveled against him.
The hearing on Romualdez’s petition for bail is still ongoing.
GMA News Online has reached out to Romualdez’s camp for comment and will publish it as soon as it becomes available. —NB, GMA News

articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has issued a suspension order on eight personnel of the Department of Public Works (DPWH) in Surigao del Norte amid the ongoing Ombudsman probe on the flood control…

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 4:23pm

The Office of the Ombudsman has issued a suspension order on eight personnel of the Department of Public Works (DPWH) in Surigao del Norte amid the ongoing Ombudsman probe on the flood control projects in the area.
Placed under preventive suspension without pay for six months at the maximum are:

items: Annie Dela Vega, DPWH Regional Office 11 District Engineer
Federico Gotico III, Engineer III of the DPWH Surigao del Norte 1st District Engineering Office (DEO)
Demilyn Castrence, Engineer III of the DPWH Surigao del Norte 1st DEO
Quintinano Armendariz Jr., Engineer III of the DPWH Surigao del Norte 1st DEO
Edward Tinio all Engineer III of the DPWH Surigao del Norte 1st DEO
Florencio Sulana, Engineer II
Acting Chief of Quality Assurance
Ricky Arciga, Engineer II
Jerome Sulapas, Accountant III

blocks.text: The Ombudsman said these individuals are facing administrative complaints over alleged conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service, grave misconduct, and serious dishonesty, and that “sufficient grounds exist to impose preventive suspension on respondents.”

“Without delving into the merits of the case and based on the evidence submitted by complainant, the allegations against Respondents appear to be supported by strong evidence at this stage,” the Ombudsman said.

The Ombudsman’s Field Investigation Office 2, acting as the complainant, alleges that substantially incomplete projects were fully paid by the DPWH under the respondents’ watch, to the detriment of the government.
The Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) earlier submitted as evidence the list of reportedly completed DPWH projects in the area, that turned out to be incomplete.

“The preventive suspension was imposed pending the resolution of the administrative cases, as a precautionary measure against possible abuse of the prerogatives of the respondents’ current offices in relation to the case,” the Ombudsman added.
GMA News Online has reached out to DPWH Region 11 for comment and will publish them as soon as it is available. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: M&S takes more than a year to recover from cyber-attack as profits bounce back to £355m
articles.summary:
Sales and profit from clothing and homeware remain below two years ago but ‘brand is in good health’

Marks & Spencer has said a

blocks.text: Marks & Spencer has said a devastating cyber-attack that shut down its website last year continued to hurt clothing sales over the summer, more than a year after the hack.

The retailer said profits bounced back to £355m in the six months to 26 September from only £3.4m a year before as it partly recovered from the hack. The attack, which began over Easter 2025, forced it to shut its website, which sells clothing and homewares, for more than six weeks.
Total sales over the half year across the food to fashion group rose 16.2% to £9.2bn.

However, M&S said sales and profit from its clothing and homewares arm remained below two years ago as “availability was constrained due to the longer than expected impact of manual ordering processes following the incident, while profitability was diluted by an increased mix of online sales which have higher fulfilment costs”.
The retailer has previously explained that its team of buyers had to calculate demand and make orders to suppliers without the help of their usual technology and detailed information last year.
Stuart Machin, the chief executive of M&S, said: “We are broadening our appeal and the brand is in good health, but the results fell short of their potential and show there is a lot more to do.”

The company said it had been able to take a bigger share of a declining clothing market despite the availability problems, which were now resolved, but “market conditions remain challenging”. Clothing, beauty and homewares sales rose 17.5% to almost £2bn in the half year compared with the same period last year, which was affected by the hack.
Performance is expected to improve in the second half as M&S said availability has now recovered “creating a better balance between core and seasonal stock”.

M&S’s food business increased sales by almost 14% to £5.2bn in the half year as it opened seven new stores and expanded or refurbished others. M&S said it was gaining share on everyday items such as meat, dairy and fresh produce after investing £50m in keeping prices down and improving quality.
after newsletter promotion
The group’s Ocado joint venture also swung to a half-year profit of £25.6m from a loss of £3.1m a year before as sales rose 16% and it improved the efficiency of its deliveries
M&S said it expected to cut £120m in costs this year across technology, logistics and stores. It said this would partly offset new costs, including £35m related to a new packaging levy.

articles.title: Sotto seeks stricter Senate rules on prolonged absences
articles.summary: Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente "Tito" Sotto has filed a resolution seeking clearer rules on the prolonged and unauthorized absences of senators, citing complaints filed before the Committee on…

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 4:14pm
Sen. Tito Sotto during the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte on Oct. 12, 2026.
Senate PRIB
MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III has filed a resolution recommending the revision of Senate rules on prolonged and unauthorized absences.
Sotto said that “such absenteeism and neglect of duty is deemed a waste of taxpayer funds,” citing complaints filed before the Committee on Ethics.
He added that public officials "must be accountable to the people they serve and must serve with utmost responsibility, integrity, loyalty and efficiency."

Four lawmakers have been absent from Senate sessions, including fugitive Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged crimes against humanity, including murder.
Serving as chief of the Philippine National Police during former President Rodrigo Duterte’s term, Dela Rosa is accused of helping carry out killings associated with Duterte’s war on drugs.
Authorities have offered a P50 million reward for information leading to his capture and intensified their manhunt following the expiration of the week-long deadline for his arrest.
Sens. Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, meanwhile, are detained at the New Quezon City Jail over separate plunder charges.
Estrada is alleged to have received kickbacks from anomalous flood control projects, while Marcoleta faces charges related to P75 million worth of undisclosed campaign donations.
Sen. Loren Legarda has similarly received complaints for plunder and graft but has been on medical leave since August 3.

All three absentee lawmakers are not currently receiving their salaries and Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses. Their regular staff, according to Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, continue to receive pay.

articles.title: Immigration intercepts 2 Filipinos bound for conflict zones
articles.summary: The Bureau of Immigration has intercepted two Filipino men attempting to leave the country after uncovering suspicious online recruitment schemes that promised thousands of dollars in salaries and…

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 3:45pm
One of the two Pinoys intercepted by the Bureau of Immigration after attempting to leave the country for alleged jobs in conflict zones.
Bureau of Immigration / Released

MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Immigration has intercepted two Filipino men attempting to leave the country after uncovering suspicious online recruitment schemes that promised thousands of dollars in salaries and signing bonuses for jobs in armed conflict zones.
In a statement on Wednesday, November 4, the bureau said the separate interceptions occurred on October 24 and October 27.
The first passenger, an unemployed former protection agent and security guard, was intercepted on October 24.

During questioning, he revealed that he had been recruited through Facebook and subsequently contacted via WhatsApp. The recruiter allegedly promised him a $12,000 (P762,174) signing bonus upon arrival, alongside a monthly salary of $2,500 (P158,778.75), with all travel expenses covered.
Three days later, on October 27, immigration officers stopped a second Filipino man who initially claimed he was traveling to Hong Kong for a vacation sponsored by a friend.

Further inquiry showed that he had also responded to a Facebook job advertisement before communicating with the recruiter via WhatsApp, where he was offered an overseas position promising a $27,000 (P1,714,810.50) upfront payment and a $3,000 (P190,534.50) monthly salary without requiring any initial out-of-pocket expenses.

The bureau noted that both cases followed a pattern of unverified recruiters using lucrative financial promises to entice victims into travel arrangements to destinations affected by active armed conflicts.
On October 17, the bureau also stopped three Filipinos in Davao who attempted to leave the country for alleged military and border guard work in Eastern Europe.

articles.title: Four tankers destroyed by naval mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran's IRGC says
articles.summary: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says the vessels had hit sea mines while trying to cross a prohibited route.

blocks.text: Four oil tankers were destroyed after hitting naval sea mines, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday, a day after US officials said the US military had launched strikes on the country.

The IRGC said two of the vessels were still burning, and two additional tankers had been seized, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. It said they were trying to travel through a prohibited southern route in the Strait of Hormuz.

The BBC has not independently verified the IRGC's claim, which came as US voters punished Republicans at the midterm elections, leading Iran's top negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, to say the results showed Americans had said no to war.
He warned Washington not to betray its public.
The IRCG also reported three tankers had been destroyed after hitting mines early on Tuesday, and that they had shot down an MQ-9 drone over the Strait.
The earlier US strikes on Qeshm were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.

Ghalibaf, who is also Iran's parliamentary speaker, posted on X, external that the midterm results showed that whether it was "conscience or the cost of living, Americans said no to war, and we endorse this message".
"If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our 'no' comes with a nightmare."

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday acknowledged the poor results for Republican congress members was partly due to the war on Iran and the consequent increased gas prices, but that he didn't regret launching it. He told the BBC's partner CBS News that the conflict would end "when I say it ends".

In an interview with the Financial Times ahead of the midterm elections on Tuesday, Trump suggested he was happy with the state of the conflict, and that he didn't consider them to be "really in a war".

Asked about comments by Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu that there would be another attack on Iran this week, Trump said they were "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".
On Tuesday night, Trump told Fox News there were some people who would "love" to do a "heavy hit" on Iran.
"The only thing I can tell you with certainty, they will never have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.
Talks to end the conflict, which was triggered by joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February, have been stalled for months, with little sign of a breakthrough.
Ghalibaf told a parliamentary session on Tuesday that Iran "will not surrender" and the responsibility to prevent a war lay with the US.

"If Washington makes another strategic mistake, it should know that this time it will face a new battlefield and will be even more desperate than it is today as it searches for a way out," Ghalibaf said.
Meanwhile Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian maintained his government had been trying to resolve the crisis "through dialogue".
"No-one will benefit from this war" if fighting is restarted, he said on Tuesday.

Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz in response to the attack, has said it will only reopen it if the US agrees to demands contained in its peace plan. Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei this week said the seven-step plan had been condensed, and could be implemented in two days if the US agreed.
