articles.title: Delhi air quality worsens ahead of Diwali as firework restrictions enter force
articles.summary: On Wednesday morning, Delhi's air quality index reading stood at 377, in the "very poor" category.

blocks.text: Delhi is once again battling worsening air pollution as the onset of winter brings a familiar deterioration in air quality.

The city's Air Quality Index (AQI) - which measures PM2.5, fine particulate matter that can clog lungs - has crossed 300, entering the "very poor" category and raising health concerns for millions of residents.
Breathing such polluted air over prolonged periods can cause respiratory problems and worsen existing illnesses, with children and older people particularly vulnerable.
Authorities have responded by invoking Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP), introducing measures to curb dust, vehicle emissions and other sources of pollution.
Delhi and neighbouring parts of northern India grapple with hazardous air every winter, particularly around Diwali, one of India's biggest festivals, which is just days away.
The festival is celebrated with lights, lamps and fireworks, which often worsen the city's already poor air quality by releasing fine particles and harmful gases into the atmosphere.

The annual pollution crisis is driven by a combination of factors, including vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, falling temperatures, low wind speeds and the burning of crop stubble in neighbouring states.
The sharp rise in pollution follows an unusually clean October, when Delhi recorded its lowest average AQI for the month in eight years.
Experts have attributed the sudden deterioration to falling temperatures, slow winds and an increase in crop-residue burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab and Haryana.
A recent storm had brought rain and stronger winds, helping clear the air. But as the weather settled, north-westerly winds returned, carrying smoke from burning fields towards the capital.
India's pollution watchdog classifies AQI readings between 301 and 400 as "very poor", while anything above 400 is considered "severe". On Wednesday morning, Delhi's AQI stood at 377.
The index takes into account eight major pollutants, including PM2.5 - tiny particles about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair that can penetrate deep into the lungs.
With Diwali just days away, there are concerns that fireworks could push pollution levels even higher.
Last year, Delhi woke up to a toxic haze the morning after the festival, despite a court directive to use less-polluting firecrackers.
Authorities have imposed restrictions on firecrackers over the years, including outright bans on their manufacture, sale and use, but enforcing them has proved difficult.
On Monday, India's Supreme Court allowed the manufacture, sale and use of certified green firecrackers in Delhi and neighbouring areas for a limited period.
It said the crackers could be set off only between 06:00 and 07:00 local time (00:30-01:30 GMT) and between 20:00 and 22:00 (14:30-16:30 GMT) on 7 and 8 November, during the Diwali weekend.
The court also banned fireworks within 300m of hospitals, care homes, schools and other designated silence zones.

Green firecrackers use modified chemical formulations designed to produce fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. They must carry QR codes that allow buyers and authorities to verify details of their manufacturer and certification.
But ensuring that only approved firecrackers are sold remains a major challenge.
In its latest order, the Supreme Court acknowledged that conventional firecrackers had continued to be sold as green alternatives, even when a complete ban was in place.
It has directed police to patrol designated sales areas, carry out random QR-code checks and seize illegal firecrackers.
During particularly severe pollution episodes, Delhi authorities have also introduced measures such as hybrid schooling, work-from-home arrangements and restrictions on certain vehicles.

The problem is not confined to the capital. Mumbai, India's financial hub, has also recorded elevated pollution levels over the past month, despite benefiting from coastal winds that typically help disperse pollutants.

On 24 October, Mumbai's AQI had reached 322, placing it in the "very poor" category. The spike was attributed to a combination of low wind speeds, construction dust, garbage burning, firecracker emissions and pollutants carried from neighbouring regions.
The city's air quality has improved in recent days - and it recorded an AQI of 89, classified as "satisfactory", on Wednesday. Neighbouring Navi Mumbai recorded a "moderate" AQI of 118.
The improvement follows nearly two weeks of smoggy conditions, with residents sharing photos and videos of the haze on social media.
Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external Twitter, external and Facebook, external.

articles.title: US midterm election results: Democrats flip House and Senate. Here's what else the data tell us
articles.summary: Though vote counts are still ongoing, Democrats have won clear majorities in both the US House and Senate. DW takes a look at who voted Republican, who voted Democrat, and what it all means.

image.caption: In the midterms, Americans vote on whether Republicans or Democrats hold the majority in CongressImage: Datajournalism Midterms 2026

blocks.text: This article was updated throughout the night. DW follows the Associated Press (AP) for when a seat is called for Republicans or Democrats.

In the 2026 midterms, Americans voted on all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 members of the Senate. Before election night, Republicans held the majority in both Congress chambers, if only by a hair.

Midterm elections are held every four years. The results will influence US politics for the next few years. Despite the significant executive power delegated to the presidency according to the US Constitution, the majority of federal political decisions have to be approved by Congress before they can be implemented.
Live election results: Democrats win majority in both House and Senate
For ongoing updates, go to our US midterms live blog.

In the US Senate, Democrats have managed to flip several Republican seats, winning races in Republican strongholds such as North Carolina, South Carolina, Kansas, Texas, and Iowa. With that, they have crossed the majority-line of 51 seats required to gain control of the chamber.

In the House of Representatives, all 435 seats are up for election. Democrats have crossed the threshold of 218 seats required to win the majority. That means they have flipped both chambers of Congress.
How did Americans vote: a look at demographics and attitudes

The data on voter demographics and attitudes is based on a representative survey of almost 80,000 verified voters conducted by survey and market research firm SSRS on behalf of AP and other news organizations. It builds on interviews of both early and mail-in voters as well as exit polls of in-person voters on Election Day. Where percentages of Republican and Democratic voters don't add up to 100%, the remaining percent were voters who voted for third-party candidates.
Republicans lead among white men, Democrats among younger voters

Republicans continue to make up the majority of white male voters. 55% of white men polled voted Republican. On the opposite end of the spectrum are Black women, 92% of whom voted Democrat. Remarkably, the majority of both Latino men and women voted Democrat in this election. Two years ago, Latinos were a big part of the vote that carried Trump to his second term in the White House.
Latino voters turn away from Republicans

The data shows that Republicans have lost support among all demographic groups compared to the last midterms in November 2022. Even among white men, the share of those who voted Republican fell from 60% to 55%. Among white women, the Republicans' share fell from 56% to 47%, and among Latinos, the percentage of Republican voters decreased as well.
Democrats lead among young, urban voters and college graduates
Age-wise, Democrats are strongest among young voters. Three-quarters of 18- to 24-year-olds voted Democrat. On the flipside, Republicans lead with 51% among voters aged 65 and up.

The urban-rural divide that has been part of US politics for years continues to hold. Among urban voters, 71% voted Democrat, among suburban voters, that number stands at 58%. On the other hand almost 60% of rural and small town voters were Republicans.
Democrats make up 62% of voters with a college degree. Among voters without a college degree, the split is less significant: 47% voted Democrat and 51% Republican.
It's the economy, stupid

One of the most important factors in this year's midterms is the economy. Prices for gas have increased significantly since the start of the Iran war, and everyday goods have become more and more expensive across the country as well. Almost half of all Americans say their family's financial situation is worse than two years ago.

That sentiment is not the same across the board though. Among those saying their family is better off than two years ago, 75% voted Republican and 24% Democrat. Among those saying they are worse off, only 24% voted Republican and 74% Democrat. President Trump has been saying that the country is on the upswing.
Immigration, economy, the state of democracy: What's the biggest issue for voters?

On the question of which issue facing the country is most crucial, voters are divided among party lines. Of those who said immigration is the most important issue, 89% voted Republican and only 10% voted Democrat. Anti-immigrant rhetoric has been a mainstay of Trump's speeches. He promised to ramp up deportations at the start of his second term. Many states have seen a sharp increase in activity from federal immigration agencies. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) agents have been arresting immigrants off the street, even people who have ongoing asylum application processes, for example. Trump and his supporters say these actions are necessary to make the US safer.

Among those who say that the state of democracy is the most pressing issue in the US, 78% voted Democrat. Congressional Democrats and their supporters have been saying they are concerned about how Trump ignores direct judicial orders, for example to halt deportations, or Congressional resolutions. Among those saying the economy is the most important issue, there's an almost even split of Republican and Democratic voters.
US Iran- and Israel policies

American voters are split on major foreign policy decisions made by the Trump administration. Among those saying that the joint US-Israeli war against Iran was the right decision, 91% were Republican and only 7% Democratic voters. Among those saying it was the wrong decision to attack Iran, 82% were Democratic voters and 16% were Republican voters.

The US support for Israel has been a highly controversial topic ever since Israel began its strikes on Gaza in retaliation to the Hamas terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. The two countries have long been partners, with the US being the most important ally for Israel, and Jewish voters a crucial demographic in the US. But as the humanitarian situation in Gaza deteriorates, support for Israel among the US population, particularly among younger people and liberals, has been wavering. Of those saying US support for Israel is too strong, 78% were Democrat voters and 20% were Republican voters. Among those saying support is about right, only one quarter was Democrat voters.
Domestic policy: dissatisfaction with Congress and country's direction

Among those dissatisfied with the House's and Senate's work, one third are Republican voters. With the extreme level of polarization in the US, reaching compromises to pass laws or approve a budget in Congress has become harder in recent years. That could be contributing to dissatisfaction.

Of people seeing their country as going in the right direction in general, only 4% were Democrat voters. Of those saying they're dissatisfied or even angry about the US's current direction, 70% were Democrat voters — and 27% Republican.

92% of those who said they approved of ICE's actions were Republican, while of those who disapproved, 86% were Democrat. Regarding Trump's tariff policy, there's a split along party lines as well, with Republican voters largely feeling they helped the economy. The president had introduced sharply increased tariffs on goods from a large number of US trading partners. Trump said the move was intended to even out unfair trade balances and protect American manufacturing. He has also used tariffs to punish countries he saw as acting against his political interests. The trade measures have made many goods more expensive for Americans.
Low approval ratings for Trump

Trump is not on the ballot, but the midterms are considered a referendum on how he and his Republicans governed the country for the past two years. Most recently, Trump's approval ratings have fallen to the lowest he has ever had, with just under 30% of Americans saying they think he is doing a good job.
In recent history, only George W. Bush has fared worse, with 25% at the end of his second term. During the 2006 midterm election, Bush's Republican Party lost control of both chambers of Congress.

articles.title: Ecstatic scenes and historic moments: What's happened so far in the midterms
articles.summary: Democrats have taken control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency - proving moments of celebration.

blocks.text: Ecstatic scenes and historic moments: What's happened so far in the midterms
How the Democratic takeover of the Senate could impact Trump
ByNardine Saad
Reporting fromLos Angeles, California
Democrats have won both the US Senate and House of Representatives, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Even before results are finalised, the night has provided some historic results and scenes of celebration. These are some of the key moments so far.
Democrats talk of 'great American comeback' after historic results

Democrats have tallied up victories in states that were comfortably won by Republican President Trump two years ago, registering sizeable swings in the likes of Texas, Kansas, Ohio and South Carolina.

Among the senior party figures who have cheered the results are Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is now poised to take over as the speaker of the lower chamber of Congress.
"Today begins the great American comeback," he told a crowd of supporters.
If Jeffries' colleagues choose to keep him as the leader of their party's delegation in House, he will be the next speaker, taking over from Republican Mike Jeffries.
Trump congratulates opposition on 'good job'
Trump has spoken throughout the night to a number of media outlets, striking a conciliatory tone and conceding that the Democrats did a "good job".

He said he would accept the results and that he was looking forward to working with the opposition party - albeit he would still have the power, as president, to veto legislation that Democrats advance through Texas.

Trump distanced himself from some of the Republican candidates who contested the election, saying: "In some cases they didn't like the candidates, and in some cases those candidates were not my friend."
Cheers as Democrats win first Senate flip of the night in North Carolina

blocks.caption: Image caption, Roy Cooper was expected to have a tough fight on his hands in North Carolina

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Roy Cooper was expected to have a tough fight on his hands in North Carolina
There were cheers from supporters in North Carolina as the Democrats secured the night's first flip of a Senate seat.
The state's former Democratic governor, Roy Cooper, won against Republican candidate Michael Whatley.
"Tonight we show the country that when everyday people come together, we can make change," Cooper said as he addressed his supporters on Tuesday.
The last time the Democrats won a Senate race in the state was 2008, despite the party making enormous investment in time and money behind their candidates in recent contests.
Keisha Lance Bottoms becomes first black female governor

blocks.caption: Image caption, Keisha Lance Bottoms beat billionaire businessman Rick Jackson,

blocks.text: Keisha Lance Bottoms beat billionaire businessman Rick Jackson,

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, has been projected to win the governor's race in Georgia, becoming the first black governor and first woman to be elected to the state's highest office.
The BBC's Carl Nasman described ecstatic scenes as the race was projected blue, which came after the state's former senator said the party was "nauseously optimistic" about their chances this year.

Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman and healthcare executive, who was endorsed by outgoing Governor Brian Kemp and President Trump, who spent $200 million of his own money on the race.
The state has also not had a Democratic governor in more than 20 years.
Ossoff victory in Georgia adds fuel to 2028 speculation

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jon Ossoff as seen as a potential future Democratic contender for the presidency

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Jon Ossoff as seen as a potential future Democratic contender for the presidency
As well as Bottoms being elected the new governor of Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff has been projected as the winner of the Senate race there, giving him a second term.
His victory was not unexpected as he had a comfortable lead in the polls over his Republican challenger Mike Collins - a member of the lower House chamber.
Ossoff told his supporters following his victory that for those who "doubted whether our republic would survive" over the last two years, the "first light of dawn is on the horizon".

Republicans had hoped this would be a more competitive race because the Peach State has been reliably Republican for decades. Trump also won it in the 2024 presidential election, after Joe Biden eked out a narrow victory there in 2020.

Now that he has won re-election in the Senate, the speculation surrounding Ossoff's plans for the next presidential election in 2028 will likely increase - he is considered a potential leading contender if he throws his hat in the ring.
Chris Pappas celebrates with husband as first openly gay man elected to Senate
Watch: "I am ready to fight" - Senator-elect Chris Pappas celebrates New Hampshire win
Democrat Chris Pappas has also made history as the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. He celebrated on stage alongside his husband in New Hampshire.
Pappas is projected to defeat former Republican Senator John Sununu in the race - who comes from one of the state's political dynasties having seen his father and brother serve as governor.

But the contest between the two was well-natured, with Pappas thanking his opponent on Tuesday by saying: "We all owe John Sununu a big debt of gratitude for his public service for the people of New Hampshire."
The 46-year-old Pappas had represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019 but chose not to run for re-election so he could launch his campaign for the Senate.

articles.title: US contractor gave Ethiopia secrets to help kill Tigray fighters
articles.summary: The Ethiopian-born American citizen admitted sharing dozens of classified documents with senior Ethiopian officials.

blocks.text: An Ethiopian-born American citizen has pleaded guilty to passing highly classified intelligence to Ethiopia, including information he hoped would help target and kill fighters during the country's 2020 civil war.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, a former US contractor, admitted sharing dozens of classified documents and photographs with senior Ethiopian officials over more than two years, the US Department of Justice said.
"In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security," said US Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.
The 54-year-old faces up to 22 years in prison under a plea agreement, with sentencing scheduled for next April.
Abraham had worked as a contractor at the State Department, Justice Department and National Reconnaissance Office, the agency responsible for US intelligence satellites.
Prosecutors said Abraham worked with senior figures in Ethiopia's political, military and intelligence establishments between 2021 and his arrest in August 2023.

He secretly removed classified material from secure government facilities, sometimes copying sensitive information into handwritten notes that he carried out of the buildings. He used his position as an IT administrator to extract electronic intelligence files.
"Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia," prosecutors said.
The information included satellite imagery and details of military activities, which he passed to Ethiopian officials through encrypted messages.
The FBI said Ethiopian officials subsequently used intelligence supplied by Abraham in military operations.
Prosecutors said he hoped the information would help Ethiopia's military identify and kill paramilitary fighters.
"Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree," said John Eisenberg, the US assistant attorney general for national security.
In one message to an Ethiopian official in December 2021, he wrote: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia," court papers showed.
Later that day, he shared further intelligence and urged the official: "Please send Dro[nes]."

The revelations shed light on how sensitive American intelligence was passed to Ethiopian authorities during a devastating civil war that killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
He was arrested in Maryland in August 2023 following an investigation into his handling of classified intelligence.
At the time, prosecutors alleged that had removed security markings from intelligence reports and shared information with a foreign intelligence official.
In one exchange, the official asked him to continue providing assistance, to which Lemma replied: "Roger that!"
Pirro, the US attorney, said Abraham had abused his access to some of America's most sensitive intelligence.
She accused him of betraying his colleagues and country with prosecutors saying he "will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law".
Abraham pleaded guilty to conspiring to transmit national defence information to a foreign government.
His sentencing is scheduled for 14 April 2027.
The two-year conflict, which began in November 2020, pitted Ethiopian federal forces and their allies against fighters from the northern Tigray region.
It was marked by widespread allegations of atrocities, including massacres, sexual violence and attacks on civilians.
A peace agreement signed in November 2022 ended the main fighting, although tensions and insecurity have persisted.

blocks.text: Here is a roundup of the biggest headlines from across India on Wednesday, November 4.
November 4, 2026
Election Commission says deleted voters can re-enroll using Form 6
The Election Commission of India on Tuesday said that voters whose names were deleted during Special Intensive Revision (SIR) can use Form 6 for inclusion in electoral rolls.
The poll body also assured that no action would be taken against people using Form 6 for re-inclusion in rolls.
The Election Commission's clarification comes as Form 6 requires applicants to declare that they are seeking inclusion in the electoral roll for the first time.
The required declaration in Form 6 had become a bone of contention after a section argued that making deleted voters submit this for re-inclusion was like forcing them to give a false declaration.
Protesters accuse India's government of rigging voter rolls
The SIR, which has resulted in the deletion of millions of voters across India, has spurred a massive controversy with the opposition alleging vote theft by the ruling Narendra Modi-led government.
The Congress Party was quick to call the latest EC communication "another deceptive word game to cover up a flawed process asking voters to make a false declaration."

No amount of damage control can fix this "flawed process," and SIR needs to be stopped, Congress Party leader Jairam Ramesh said, adding, "each damage control attempt shows how badly designed the SIR process is."

articles.title: James Talarico becomes first Democrat to win Texas Senate seat since 1988
articles.summary: "This wasn't just a tsunami, not just a referendum, but this was a bloodbath," one expert told the BBC on Democrats' historic wins in Texas.

blocks.text: Democrat James Talarico has won a key Senate race in Texas, in what is likely the single biggest upset for Republicans in this year's elections.

Talarico's stunning victory over Republican Ken Paxton marks the first time a Democrat has won a US Senate seat in Texas since 1988 - and has helped solidify Democrats taking full control of the US Congress in a tidal wave of wins across America.
Talarico, a former schoolteacher, was a little-known figure until last year. He made the rising cost of living under Republican leadership a central theme of his run.
Paxton sought to portray Talarico's views as too progressive for the state, and campaigned alongside Trump on several occasions.

items: FOLLOW LIVE: Election results and analysis of the US midterms
LIVE RESULTS: Follow live results as they come into the BBC
ANALYSIS: Democrats eye sweeping gains and reshaping of political map

blocks.text: Supporters of Talarico went berserk as TVs at a watch party in Austin, the state's capitol, projected him the winner.
They hugged, they kissed, and they drank to a reality that many say they dared not believe would come true.
Emerging on stage to rapturous applause at his official watch party at a nearby performing arts theatre, Talarico pronounced: "We just took back Texas."
"We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas," he continued, referring to his win over Paxton whose campaign was backed by Elon Musk, the world's richest man.
He invoked religious themes that have grown familiar to his campaign, comparing his unlikely odds to the biblical story of David and Goliath.
"This win, this win is for every Texan who's ever wondered if anyone is listening," he said. "I hear you, we hear you. And tonight the world hears you."
For decades, the idea of a Democrat winning a statewide race had felt like a pipe dream for Texas liberals.
As the nation's second most populous state, Texas has been a bastion of conservatism, routinely rolling out Republican policies that are later employed elsewhere.
But throughout the campaign, polls suggested state legislator Talarico was breaking through with voters, energising a Texas Democratic base desperate for new leadership.
Spending in the race skyrocketed, and it quickly grew to become the most expensive US Senate race in history, with more than half a billion dollars spent.
Billionaire Elon Musk poured in $158m (£117m) to a super PAC supporting Paxton's campaign - a point that Talarico used in attacks on Paxton's campaign.
Then two members of the Bush family, the Republican political dynasty that counts Texas as its political launchpad, backed Talarico in a stunning move foreshadowing Paxton's doom.
George Washington University political science professor Quardricos Driskell told the BBC that Paxton was a major part of Republicans' downfall, calling him an "objectively terrible candidate".

He said the win in Texas by Talarico, combined with another upset on Tuesday that ousted the state's Republican governor Greg Abbott, was "absolutely historic". Abbott's loss marked the first time a Democrat had won a race for governor in the state since the 1990s.

"This wasn't just a tsunami, not just a referendum, but this was a bloodbath," Driskell said about Democrats gains in the Lone Star State. "A clear distinction that the country wants to go in a different direction".

Talarico defeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary. Then continued to maintain good polling numbers despite an onslaught of negative adverts, including attacks on past comments where he supported transgender people.

Throughout his campaign, he frequently leaned into his religious upbringing – as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary – sprinkling his stump speeches with biblical references.
Paxton had been beleaguered by a number of political scandals, including his impeachment by his own party in 2023 on corruption accusations, before he was later acquitted by the state's Senate.
He was also indicted by the US Securities and Exchange Commission on federal fraud charges, but they were later dismissed.
Trump made multiple stops in Texas to beef up support for Paxton and other Republicans - including in reliably-Republican spots, signalling how concerned party leadership was about turnout.
Voters have been frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war.
Hispanic voters and those who live along the southern US border have also taken issue with Trump's immigration policies.

Despite border crossings plummeting under Trump - something that had been popular with Texas voters - polls suggested Trump's support among Hispanics, who make up a third of the state's population, had ebbed significantly.

Surveys taken since late summer indicated a majority of Texan Hispanic voters - many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 - now disapproved of the president. They also suggested that Hispanic voters were favouring Democrats over Republicans by a significant margin.

Many Texas Hispanics who spoke to the BBC before the election pointed to Trump's immigration crackdown as the reasoning behind their change of heart. They pointed to aggressive measures that led to citizens being detained and non-violent offenders being rounded up indiscriminately.

articles.title: From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated
articles.summary: Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find…

image.caption: From rotten food and sexual behavior to political beliefs, researchers want to know how different forms of disgust relate to our attitudesImage: picture alliance

blocks.text: Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.
One explanation begins with evolution.
"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.
What are the three types of disgust?
But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

items: Pathogen disgust: Reactions to potential sources of infection, such as rotten food, vomit or bodily waste.
Sexual disgust: Reactions to particular sexual behaviors or situations.
Moral disgust: Reactions to wrongdoing, such as betrayal or cruelty. Researchers debate whether this reflects physical revulsion or moral disapproval.

blocks.text: One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump used language evoking contagion when describing immigrants early in his 2024 presidential campaignImage: Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.
"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."
Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.
"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.
Do liberals and conservatives feel disgust differently?
Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.
A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.
However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.
Can our bodies reveal our politics?
Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.
Many US voters are undecided, disillusioned or disengaged
But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.
Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.
"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.
How do gut feelings influence political beliefs?
Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.
"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."
The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."
They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.
But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.
What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

blocks.caption: Pathogen disgust is one type of disgust thought to have evolved to protect us from infectionImage: Elena Shishkina/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: "People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.
Can disgust actually be measured?
Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.
He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.
Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.
"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.
The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.
Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."
How might politicians exploit feelings of disgust?
Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.
"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.
Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?
"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.
Does disgust influence how people vote?

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.
"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.
Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.
"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."
Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.
He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.
"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said.

articles.title: Florida Republicans fend off Democrats as state elects first black governor
articles.summary: Republican Byron Donalds, who was backed by President Donald Trump, will be the first black governor of Florida.

items: FOLLOW LIVE - Election results and analysis
RESULTS - Live US 2026 midterm results as they come in
ANALYSIS - Democrats push deep into Republican territory with historic wins

blocks.text: Nixon scored a surprise win in the Democratic primary to become her party's standard-bearer, although her campaign funding could not match Moody's.
Donalds had served in Congress since 2021 before running for governor, to replace long-serving Republican Governor Ron DeSantis, who was term limited and could not run again.
A big supporter of Trump, Donalds was at one point on the short list to be his running mate in 2024.
Born in Brooklyn, he moved to Florida for university and became a fixture in local politics before running for Congress.

Democrats in the state had some surprise wins, too. Republicans in Florida had helped redraw political voting maps as part of a national redistricting push to boost each political party's chances of taking seats in the House.
But in all three districts that were redrawn to help Republicans, Democrats held onto their seats.

articles.title: How America voted in maps and charts
articles.summary: See the maps and charts that show how America voted in the US midterm elections.

blocks.text: How America voted in maps and charts
ByWesley Stephenson
Data Journalist
It's been an extraordinary night for the Democrats so far in the US midterms.
They have taken control of the Senate and are projected to take control of the House of Representatives too, according to the BBC's partner CBS News.
Senate

The results in the Senate are beyond what the Democrats would have expected. North Carolina was a likely pick-up but South Carolina was a huge shock and Kansas had not returned a Democratic senator since 1932.
Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine have also turned blue. There is one toss-up seat to come in Alaska and even Mississippi is now on a knife edge, according to CBS News.
Polls before the election saw South Carolina as leaning Republican. It had been a deep red seat for many years, last returning a Democratic senator in 1998.
House

The BBC's partner CBS News projected the Democrats would win the House just after 03:00 GMT on Wednesday (22:00 EST Tuesday). The Democrats are making the gains they need to take control but have their sights set on a much bigger victory.
Two significant seats are Florida 14 and Florida 25 which the Democrats have held. This is a blow to the Republicans' attempt to redraw the boundaries in their favour.
The redistricting saw both districts move from having a majority of 2024 Kamala Harris voters to having a majority of people who voted for Donald Trump.
Florida 22, which was also redrawn to favour the Republicans, saw a victory for the Democrats too.
Hispanic voters turn to Democrats in Florida

Hispanic voters look to be one of the key groups in the elections in Florida. A huge poll of voters suggests that this group backed the Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon by 55% to 44% for the Republican Ashley Moody.
This is a turnaround from the estimated 55% of Hispanic voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024.
The poll also asked what issues voters were most concerned about. It suggests that across the country the economy was the biggest issue, followed by the state of democracy.
When voters were asked if Donald Trump's policies impacted economic conditions, the poll suggests more that two-thirds believe they had made things worse.
Produced by Wesley Stephenson, Christine Jeavans, Daniel Wainwright, Becky Dale, Libby Rogers, Jess Carr, John Walton and Rob England.

articles.title: UBC prof testifies she acted as a 'conduit' for sex assault allegations against Steven Galloway
articles.summary: Anabel Lyon, director of the University of British Columbia's school of creative writing, said she believed the unfounded accusations of a former student who accused bestselling author Steven…

image.caption: Writer Steven Galloway is pictured in his former office at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver on March 31, 2014. He is is suing his accuser and others in a defamation trial. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Anabel Lyon, director of the University of British Columbia's school of creative writing, said she believed the unfounded accusations of a former student who accused bestselling author Steven Galloway of sexual assault.
Annabel Lyon said she was Galloway's colleague when a former grad student accused him of sexual assault
The defamation trial brought by bestselling author Steven Galloway heard testimony Tuesday from the current head of the University of British Columbia's school of creative writing.
Annabel Lyon was called as the defence's first witness and testified she was Galloway's colleague and friend when a former graduate student accused him of sexual assault in November 2015.

Galloway is suing his accuser, known as A.B., claiming she ruined his reputation and career by circulating the unfounded allegations. Three others who also shared the allegations on social media and elsewhere are defendants at the trial.

Lyon testified that she was A.B.'s secondary thesis supervisor or "reader" in 2013 when A.B. submitted an incomplete thesis for graduation. Lyon said when she expressed her concerns to A.B.'s primary adviser, Keith Maillard, she was told A.B. should pass regardless.

"I reached out to Professor Maillard and said, 'I'm not comfortable with this, it's not a complete thesis for our purposes' … He said, 'She really needs to graduate, can you please sign off on it,'" said Lyon.
"I, to this day, regret having done that."

items: Sexual assault claims 'flat out never happened,' ex-UBC professor tells defamation trial
Sex assault allegations diminished performance of Steven Galloway's books: industry expert

blocks.text: Galloway testified earlier that he and A.B., who cannot be named under a publication ban, had a two-year affair while both were married that ended in 2013.
UBC first suspended Galloway in late 2015 citing "serious allegations" and later fired him.
A retired judge hired by UBC to conduct an investigation found that on a balance of probabilities he had not committed sexual assault.
The university later paid Galloway close to $240,000 after two arbitration processes.
Lyon said she believed A.B.'s accusations and spoke to her on the phone about the claims.
Under cross-examination, Lyon said that A.B. asked her to share the accusations, along with an assertion that she would take her story to national media if UBC didn't act against Galloway.

items: Agent of author Steven Galloway says sex assault allegations derailed promising career
'Outrageous' rhetoric alleged in emails as Steven Galloway defamation trial continues

blocks.text: Lyon said she shared what A.B. asked her to at meetings with faculty and other high-level UBC officials. Lyon said she never attempted to verify the information, nor did she feel it was her position to "edit or curate" what A.B. told her.
"I did as [A.B.] asked me to," said Lyon. "I saw myself as a conduit for the information."
Lyon said she also informed UBC administrators of an unsubstantiated report stating that 19 other students had complaints about Galloway.

The report was compiled by former student Chelsea Rooney, who claimed she had been sexually harassed by Galloway. Although she was no longer a student, Rooney acted as investigator, coming up with 19 complaints in a day.
Bestselling author Steven Galloway's defamation trial in 4th week
Lyon said she shared Rooney's report at a meeting in the dean's office "because the university asked me to be that person."
The professor was one of over 20 named defendants when Galloway filed the defamation lawsuit in 2018. She has since come to a confidential out-of-court settlement.
A handful of former defendants, including Rooney, have issued public statements of apology to Galloway.
A.B. is not testifying at the trial, and the court has heard she is not defending the alleged defamatory statements as true.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Karin Larsen is a former Olympian and award-winning sports broadcaster who covers news and sports for CBC Vancouver.

articles.title: BJMP probes alleged ‘irregularities’ in Romualdez’s detention

Former House Speaker Martin Romualdez in a Facebook video.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology said that it is investigating the irregularities that allegedly occurred in the detention of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
In a statement on Wednesday, November 4, the BJMP said that Chief Jail Director Efren Nemeño ordered an immediate investigation after rumours that Romualdez has been going out of prison.
“The investigation is ongoing. The BJMP reiterates that all PDL are subject to the same custodial rules and that any movement outside the jail requires a proper court order,” the BJMP said.
“We welcome relevant information from the public and will cooperate with any investigation by other government agencies,” it added.

According to initial CCTV verification by the BJMP National Headquarters, the Quezon City Jail–Male Dormitory experienced no power or feed interruptions, and Romualdez was not observed moving outside the facility throughout the examined timeframe.
The statement from the jail bureau came after a Facebook post by journalist Mon Tulfo, which said that Romualdez has been going out of prison by ambulance.
Romualdez has been in prison in Quezon City for a P7.44-billion non-bailable plunder case linked to flood control projects.

articles.title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
articles.summary:
Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts

The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s…

blocks.text: The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.

The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls show it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.
Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.
Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery.

Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week, has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.

blocks.caption: An ANC poster in Langa township in Cape Town. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters

blocks.text: Johannesburg, Ekurhuleni and Tshwane are in Gauteng, South Africa’s most populous and densely populated province and its economic engine. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance is leading the polls in all three metros but has not been polling above 40%.

The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media, mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs with a combination of the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters and the populist Patriotic Alliance and ActionSA across the province’s three metros.

blocks.caption: Helen Zille is campaigning to become mayor of Johannesburg. Photograph: Kim Ludbrook/EPA

blocks.text: In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to controversial past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town, which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.

The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.

blocks.caption: Jacob Zuma addresses an election rally in KwaMashu, north of Durban, on Sunday. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma is polling above 40%. The 84-year-old Zuma, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.
The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.

South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.

articles.title: Prosecutors asks ICC to admit testimonies detailing police’s ‘modus operandi’
articles.summary: In a motion filed under Rule 68(3) of the ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Office of the Prosecutor requested authorization to introduce the prior recorded statements, interview transcripts,…

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 11:57am

MANILA, Philippines — Prosecutors at the International Criminal Court have asked Trial Chamber III to admit written witness testimonies alleging systemic police tactics and fabricated accounts during the war on drugs of detained former President Rodrigo Duterte.

In a motion filed under Rule 68(3) of the ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Office of the Prosecutor requested authorization to introduce the prior recorded statements, interview transcripts, and associated case materials of four key witnesses into the official court record.
The submission focuses on establishing the operational patterns of the Philippine National Police (PNP) during drug operations.

According to court documents, the witness statements provide detailed accounts of police officers allegedly planting firearms and methamphetamine, locally known as “shabu," near victims' bodies to simulate self-defense scenarios, commonly framed in official reports as “nanlaban” incidents.

The documents filed by the prosecution further outline how official PNP reports were routinely fabricated and submitted internally as positive "accomplishments," alongside the deployment of paid police assets and financial incentives for officers involved in extrajudicial executions.

Trial Chamber III is scheduled to open the trial proper on November 30, where the former chief executive faces three counts of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder during his tenure as Davao City Mayor and as president of the Philippines.
The prosecution has also asked the court to admit testimonies of other witnesses, which are expected to be 60 to 70, according to the prosecution.
RELATED: Duterte ICC trial: Prosecutors seek to admit three witness accounts
Testimonies
The prosecution's motion centers on the written testimonies of four key witnesses, each providing critical evidence regarding different operational facets of Duterte’s drug war.
Witness P-1136
Witness P-1136 indicated that Duterte targeted public officials as "high-value targets" who were allegedly involved in the illegal drug trade.
He also stated that these targeted individuals were often recorded on the presidential drug watchlist, known as the “PRRD List.”

Furthermore, the prosecution highlighted that Witness P-1136 provided evidence going toward proof of Duterte's policy to "neutralize" local public officials allegedly involved with illegal drugs, as well as his public threats directed against high-value targets.

“P-1136 was [REDACTED]. In his statement, P-1136 indicates that Mr Duterte targeted public officials as “high-value targets” (“HVT”) allegedly involved in the illegal drug trade,a nd often recorded in the PRRD List,” the prosecution said.
Witness P-1345
According to the prosecution, witness P-1345 detailed specific patterns in police modus operandi during anti-illegal drug operations in Manila, particularly under "One Time Big Time" drives.
The witness indicated that police officers routinely planted shabu and firearms near victims' bodies to simulate self-defense scenarios and justify the killings.

Additionally, Witness P-1345 provided evidence regarding the practice of "red-tagging," noting that administration critics, labor leaders, and members of the judiciary were systematically labeled as drug personalities or subversives.

“P-1345 describes: (i) the structure and functioning [REDACTED]; (ii) the establishment of an Extrajudicial Killing (“EJK”) [REDACTED] due to an escalation in the killings;19 and (iii) the lack of cooperation from the PNP during [REDACTED]. P-1345’s statement includes detailed discussions of nine case files [REDACTED] of PNP killings of alleged drug personalities during the “war on drugs”. P-1345 identifies patterns in the modus operandi of PNP killings, including planting shabu and guns near the victim’s body. P-1345 also explains that journalists, human rights groups, labour leaders and judges who opposed Mr Duterte’s administration were ‘red-tagged’ as drug personalities or communists.”
Witness P-1391
Witness P-1391 also detailed institutional patterns within police operations, stating that official PNP reports were routinely fabricated following anti-drug operations.
The witness indicated that police deployed paid assets to carry out executions and offered monetary incentives to officers for carrying out killings.
Additionally, Witness P-1391 provided direct evidence regarding specific charged events, including Incidents 21 and 30, which involved the aftermath of the killing of 17-year-old Kian delos Santos.

“P-1391’s evidence further assists with the proof of Incidents 21 and 30. As such, the Four Witnesses’ evidence goes to the proof of the contextual elements of crimes against humanity and to the policy to ‘neutralise’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines,” the prosecution said.
Witness P-1404

According to the prosecution's filing, witness P-1404 detailed community-level surveillance mechanisms, stating that local barangay clearance policies and inter-agency efforts were used to systematically track individuals on drug watchlists.

The witness indicated that local officials were directed through the Department of the Interior and Local Government to submit updated drug watchlists on a monthly basis and to utilize community monitoring programs like “MASA MASID.”
Additionally, Witness P-1404 highlighted internal police reporting practices, noting that police officers routinely recorded and presented extrajudicial killings as official accomplishments.

“P-1404 also provides evidence on: barangay clearance policy; the different types of watchlist (including PDEA, barangay, PNP, [REDACTED] Department of Interior and Local Government (“DILG”) and Presidential); how the Co-Perpetrators ordered barangay captains via the DILG to submit updated watchlists each month; and the MASA MASID programme.He speaks about the process [REDACTED]. [REDACTED]. He also [REDACTED] and evidences reporting and the presentation of killings as “accomplishments”. P-1404’s Prior Recorded Testimony goes to proof of a policy to ‘neutralise’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines. It also provides evidence of barangay clearance policy, including [REDACTED].”

articles.title: Weapon or wine bottle? China disputes reports of artillery shell in Papua New Guinea
articles.summary: Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the 32kg object was "merely a dummy".

blocks.text: Chinese authorities have dismissed reports that a suspected China-made artillery shell was found in a commercial shipping container in Papua New Guinea, saying it is a "shell-shaped wine bottle".
"It poses no danger at all," the Chinese embassy wrote in a Facebook post on Tuesday, drawing skeptical comments.
Police in Port Moresby arrested four Chinese nationals last Friday after the 32kg object was found at a construction site in the capital city.
Authorities were looking into whether it was a live device, local reports said then, with police commissioner David Manning describing it as "a very concerning discovery".

In a report on Wednesday, the Australia Broadcasting Corporation cited unnamed sources identifying the object as an undetonated 130mm Chinese Type 59 Artillery Projectile that contains chemical explosives and a fuse. The BBC has not independently verified this.
Papua New Guinea police had earlier dismissed speculation that the object was "merely a dummy", local newspaper Post Courier said.
However, the Chinese embassy said in its statement that it is "virtually impossible" for an illegal military-grade artillery shell to be smuggled out of China to Papua New Guinea.
"China enforces some of the world's strictest firearm control laws and regulations," it wrote, adding that China is "widely recognised as one of the safest countries globally".
Some Facebook users appear unconvinced.
"What sort of wine bottle weighs 32 kilograms?" wrote one of them.
Another wrote that the object bore no labels indicating that it's a wine bottle.

articles.title: C5 rehabilitation to start in late November, target completion by early 2028
articles.summary: The P2.5 billion rehabilitation of Circumferential Road 5 (C5) will begint this November and is projected to end in early 2028

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 11:21am
Circumferential Road 5 (C5) passes through various cities in Metro Manila, including business district Makati City.
Canva / Mel Casipit
MANILA, Philippines — Rehabilitation of Circumferential Road 5 (C5) begins this November, with construction set to finish by early 2028, according to the Department of Public Works and Highways.

The 23-kilometer C5 road rehabilitation project from Kalayaan Interchange to Commonwealth Avenue is set to begin in the last week of November, Public Works Secretary Giovanni Lopez confirmed in an interview on Tuesday, November 3.

Based on the project's scope work, the rehabilitation will include base correction and asphalt overlay to improve the safety of the major thoroughfare. The project will also include widened sidewalks for pedestrians and cyclists, Lopez said.

It will take "more or less around 420 calendar days," Lopez said. If construction starts on time by late November, the project will be completed by February or the last week of January 2028, the DPWH chief added.
The northbound section of the C5 Boni Serrano Flyover was closed over Undas weekend for asphalt patching, lane marking, repainting of fences and installation of additional road delineators.
Structural strengthening work is also underway at the Pasig Boulevard-C5 Flyover in Barangay Bagong Ilog.
C5 covers various cities in Metro Manila, with pathways leading to central business districts like Ortigas Center, Bonifacio Global City and Makati City.

Construction work will take place from 10 p.m. to 4 a.m. to prevent disrupting the flow of traffic, as was done during the first phase of the Epifanio de los Santos Avenue (EDSA) rehabilitation project.
Rehabilitation of C5 is valued at P2.5 billion and is funded by unused funds from the initial P17-billion budget for EDSA.

articles.title: NBI prepares subpoenas in Bulacan pet crematoriums probe
articles.summary: PAWS said it had gathered 191 affidavits and submissions from pet owners as of November 3.

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 11:01am
NBI Director Melvin Matibag in the witness stand at the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte on July 22, 2026.
Senate PRIB
MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is preparing to issue subpoenas as it investigates the alleged dumping of pet remains in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.
NBI Director Melvin Matibag announced the move during a Tuesday, November 3 meeting with pet owners and representatives of non-government organizations assisting in the investigation.
"We can subpoena the personalities. Yung tao at saka yung dokumento nila. Definitely, dapat may record 'yan," Matibag said.
(We can subpoena the people involved and their documents. Definitely, there should be records.)
Matibag said investigators were looking into possible estafa and violations of environmental laws, among other liabilities, over the alleged improper disposal of animal remains.
He also described the alleged conduct as a betrayal of public trust.
Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) Executive Director Anna Cabrera, meanwhile, said the organization had gathered 191 affidavits and submissions from pet owners.
Of these, 25 pet owners had retrieved their pets' remains, while 12 had formally sought PAWS' assistance.
The investigation began after the remains of 26 dogs and three cats were found in plastic bags along a roadside in San Jose del Monte City.
Following the discovery, the Bacoor City government ordered the closure of Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium.
Bacoor Mayor Strike Revilla also directed the Philippine National Police to investigate the establishment's owner and pursue appropriate charges.

articles.title: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats eye sweeping gains and reshaping of political map
articles.summary: Two Senate races that a year ago were thought to be battlegrounds turned out to be slam-dunks for the Democrats.

blocks.text: This is already shaping up to be a very good night for Democrats, with much of the vote counted in the eastern United States and polls closing in key Midwestern battleground states.

Two Senate races that a year ago were thought to be battlegrounds have turned out to be slam dunks for the Democrats - Jon Ossoff's re-election race in Georgia and the open Republican-held seat in North Carolina.

That North Carolina contest, where former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper bested Republican Party insider Michael Whatley, was the first of the four pick-ups Democrats need in order to wrest control of the Senate.
Attention has now turned to Republican-held Senate seats in Texas, Kansas and Ohio, where counting is taking place.
In South Carolina, the BBC's US partner CBS News is rating the Senate race as leaning Democrat, which would be an earth-shaking result.
If you look at key races in House of Representatives, there are other encouraging signs for Democrats.
In Florida, Republicans in the state legislature had redrawn the boundaries of three Democratic-held seats to make it much easier to for them to win.
They lost all three.

items: US midterm elections results 2026
Live updates

blocks.text: Other House races in the state, where Republicans expected to win by comfortable margins, have turned out to be dogfights.
Democrats flipped an open seat in western North Carolina, for instance, and appear in position to make gains in Virginia, Kentucky and Indiana.
In races considered toss-ups across the east, Democrats are poised for the kind of victories that will help secure a House majority for the first time since 2022.
They're doing it on the back of high Democratic turnout, particularly by black voters in the south, and winning back Hispanic voters in Florida who had supported the Republicans just two years ago.
In majority black South Carolina counties, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews is significantly outperforming Kamala Harris's presidential numbers in 2024.
And in Miami-Dade County, which Trump carried that year, Democratic candidates are back on top.

articles.title: Killer who escaped Tennessee prison captured after week-long manhunt
articles.summary: Jacob Allen Morley was serving a life sentence for murder before he escaped over a prison fence.

blocks.text: US authorities have recaptured a convicted murderer who escaped a Tennessee prison more than a week ago.

Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was serving a life sentence over the killing of his colleague in 2022, when he escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, about 90 miles (145 km) north of Memphis.

The Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC) said security footage showed Morley, wearing his prison uniform, breaching the prison fence around 11:30pm on 25 October, and later stealing a vehicle from a nearby farm.
On Wednesday the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) announced Morley was in custody after an operation that involved local, state and federal agencies.
In a statement, the TBI said authorities had received a tip that Morley was hiding on an Illinois property, from which a truck had also been stolen.
The truck's licence plate was then tracked through automatic plate-reader technology, travelling through Missouri, where local authorities were dispatched to follow.

Morley was apprehended by Missouri State Highway Patrol "without incident" in Carroll County at 11:34am local time on Tuesday. Three firearms that had previously been reported stolen were also recovered from the vehicle, the TBI said.
Photos published by authorities showed Morley handcuffed and being led out of a field by officers.
Morley was convicted of first-degree murder over the death of his colleague Cody Birchfield in 2022. He was sentenced in June 2025. His request for a new trial was denied in May.
Birchfield's body was found in a metal box under Morley's home, according to Carter County court records reviewed by the BBC.
Birchfield died "as a result of a gunshot wound to the back of the head", a pathology report cited in court said. Bullet casings matched a gun found in Morley's house.

Birchfield's sister said in her victim impact statement to the court that the pair had developed a friendship while Birchfield was training Morley at the pallet manufacturing company where they were both employed.
Besides murder, Morley was also convicted of vandalism, tampering with evidence, aggravated burglary, and evading arrest.
This is not the first time Morley has led law enforcement officials on a manhunt. His 2022 arrest came after a police chase that crossed state lines into North Carolina.
The Northwest Correctional Complex is a men's prison with the capacity to hold up to 1,776 inmates, from low security to maximum, the BBC's partner CBS reported.
CBS said the prison has seen numerous acts of violence in recent years, and in July a grand jury returned dozens of indictments over assaults on staff and the murders of five inmates.

articles.title: 2024 heatwave linked to 585 more preterm births in Philippines — study
articles.summary: Extreme heat in April 2024 resulted in 585 additional preterm births during the 15-day period, where temperatures rose 2.44 degrees above normal.

blocks.text: Climate and Environment
November 4, 2026 | 10:07am
A mother holds her baby born in a leap year at a maternity hospital in Manila on February 29, 2024.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Nearly 600 more babies were born too early in the Philippines during the April 2024 heatwave, a new study estimates, as the country heads into another stretch of extreme heat under a strong El Niño.

Zero Carbon Analytics, an international think tank on climate change and the energy transition, estimates an additional 585 babies were born preterm during the 15-day extreme heat event, a 10% increase above average April figures.
The World Health Organization defines "preterm births" as those occurring before 37 weeks.

Temperatures during the 15-day spell ran 2.44 degrees Celsius above normal. At its peak, the town of Iba, Zambales logged a heat index of 53 degrees Celsius, one of the highest readings of the year at the time.

Climate change, according to the organization, caused the pre-monsoon weather to be 1.2 degrees hotter, leading to a separate estimate of 263 preterm births that would not have occurred without human-caused warming.

Zero Carbon Analytics compared the Philippines' statistics for April 2024 to the country's average April based on data from 1991 to 2020, following a baseline established by the World Meteorological Organization. Results were reported at a 95% confidence level.
Calabarzon saw the highest nominal increase at 100 births, closely followed by Metro Manila and Central Luzon with around 80 births each.
Cagayan Valley, however, had the highest rise in risk: Cagayan province experienced temperatures 4.01 degrees hotter than normal, resulting in a 17% surge.

Babies born too early are more prone to breathing problems, infections, difficulty feeding and trouble keeping warm, according to the World Health Organization. Complications of preterm birth are the leading cause of death among children under five worldwide, and many survivors live with lifelong disabilities, including learning difficulties and problems with sight and hearing.
A nation at risk
The Philippines was ranked seventh in Germanwatch's Climate Risk Index, meaning that heat-specific exposure is rising faster in the country than in most parts of the world.

Between 2020 and 2024, the country experienced 36 days with maximum temperatures above a threshold linked to increased preterm birth risk. Climate change is thought to be responsible for 30 of these days, given that a 1-degree increase in temperature is associated with 4% higher odds of preterm birth.
Women and newborns living in poverty are especially vulnerable due to limited access to healthcare, mobility, and resources to support traditional livelihoods.

The Climate Change Commission warned that temperatures could reach 45 to 50 degrees in treeless urban areas during Super El Niño, which began in October 2026. The weather pattern is expected to last until March 2027 and has already brought drought conditions to various provinces in the country.
